mechanisms.title: Record the real model transcript once and replay it keylessly as the only mocked boundary
mechanisms.problem: Model output is nondeterministic and unavailable to fork PRs, but hand-authored transcripts drift from the production agent loop and a fully mocked model boundary hides assembly regressions. The source postmortem recorded a keyless green while a real ACP session crashed, so a suite that self-skips without a key can report green without exercising anything.
triggers: A scenario must cover assembled loop, tools, persistence or UI behavior that depends on model output.
A prompt, tool schema or model-visible prefix changes and the committed expected output must change.
A suite is about to add a mock for anything other than the model.
obligations: Record fixtures against the real API under an explicit record mode, then replay them with no key in the default gate.
Keep exactly one mocked boundary: the model stream. Agent loop, tools, presenters, persistence and transport stay production implementations.
Commit the recorded per-session logs and the normalized expected outputs; regenerate only through the explicit record or refresh workflow.
A record invocation without a key must self-skip, never silently produce an empty or green fixture.
PR CI must run replay only and must never run record or refresh.
actors: Scenario author: records against the real API and reviews captured fixtures.
Reviewer: reviews the expected-output diff.
CI: replays keylessly and compares.
Maintainer: owns the API key and record workflow.
steps: Write the scenario with production composition except the model adapter.
Run `pnpm run test:snapshot:record` with a key and capture `session[.vN].jsonl` plus the wire output.
Derive one replay script from each durable `assistant/message` or `assistant/attempt` settlement.
Normalize volatile identifiers, paths and timestamps; write expected outputs.
Replay with `DSH_SNAPSHOT=replay` (web lane `test:web:ci` also injects it) and confirm no writes occur.
After an intentional product change, run refresh, review every golden diff, then replay again.

enforcement.implementation: Dedicated keyed workflow or record command separate from the keyless PR gate; record self-skips without a key; web gate registers `test:web:ci` with `DSH_SNAPSHOT=replay`; `ci.yml` never runs record or refresh.
enforcement.trust: The recorded transcript is ground truth for model behavior. The test asserts the rest of the stack around it.
enforcement.failure: Missing key during record is a skip, not a fabricated fixture. A replay mismatch fails the gate. Missing refresh fails in the same PR that changed the assembly.
exceptions: Authored override scenarios (`replay.override.json`) may drive error or cancel behavior without a model call; the session log then holds the expected log.
A scenario with no model turn may be authored keylessly, but its events must still come from the real code path.

mechanisms.applicability: Protocol-shaped and assembled-application testing where model behavior is the only genuinely nondeterministic input and a real API key can be held outside untrusted PR execution.
relationships: Depends on expected-output-authority for the comparison discipline.
Uses fixture-hygiene-guards to keep fixtures closed and current.

migration.strategy: Introduce the replay boundary before adding scenarios; separate the keyed record workflow from the always-available gate.
migration.implementation: A replay adapter keyed by caller session, a harness that harvests every session log, normalization helpers, and explicit record/refresh/replay modes.
migration.requiredSupport: A secret store usable only on trusted events, a keyless replay path, and a review process for golden diffs.

positive: A recorded scenario replays keylessly and matches its committed expected outputs.
Nested and fork scenarios route each child to its own recorded script.
rejection: Tampering a hook config output turns its scenario red on replay because the hook process still runs for real.
Removing the seed-boundary slice turns both fork scenarios red.
recovery: Refresh regenerates expected outputs only after an intentional change and the reviewer re-runs replay to prove no writes.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes as local runs or CI run ids; not re-executed during this extraction.

limitations: A recorded model reaction is one sample, not a distribution; it does not prove model quality.
Fixtures age and must be re-recorded when the model or prompt changes.
A keyless skip in the wrong workflow can still look green; the preflight in no-false-green-preflight is required.

mechanisms.title: Make committed normalized expected outputs the assertion authority, with refresh as a separate reviewed action
mechanisms.problem: A snapshot mechanism that rewrites its own expected output during the test cannot assert anything: it turns the oracle into a generator. Hand-authored event sequences also drift from the production loop while presentation tests stay green.
triggers: A snapshot test is added or changed.
A rendering, wire or persisted-log normalization changes.
A developer is tempted to run refresh in CI or inside the assertion.
obligations: Compare the live normalized result against a committed expected output; do not write expected outputs on the comparison path.
Keep refresh as a separate explicit developer action followed by review and a replay run that proves no writes.
Normalize only volatile facts (ids, paths, timestamps, durations); never collapse two distinct rendered facts into one token.
Keep expected outputs reviewable: split large prompt and tool-schema pins into Markdown and JSON sidecars, and keep text and style separate for terminal projections.
When an expected output changes, the diff must belong to the change under review.
actors: Test author: produces and explains the expected output.
Reviewer: verifies the diff represents the intended behavior.
CI: compares in replay mode and refuses to write.
steps: Choose the semantic projection that states the contract (for example rows, wrap markers and non-default styles for a terminal; aria tree for a web page).
Normalize volatile values with explicit tokens.
Commit the expected output beside the fixture.
Run replay and confirm byte equality without writes.
On intentional change, run refresh, inspect every diff, and re-run replay.

enforcement.mode: test design plus CI mode policy
enforcement.implementation: Session logs use plain equality rather than file-snapshot updates; expected-output files are committed; CI runs replay only; pin sidecars are regenerated from the normalized live header sequence rather than hand-edited.
enforcement.trust: The committed expected output is the reviewable oracle. The normalizer is trusted only for the narrow volatile fields it owns.
enforcement.failure: A mismatch fails the test. A stale expected output fails in the same PR that changed the assembly. A refresh accidentally enabled in CI would convert a regression into a passing update, so mode injection is explicit.
exceptions: Authored override scenarios may commit the expected session log as `session.jsonl` when an override file drives the model.
A transient renderer state may be authored directly because a completed log cannot retain it.

mechanisms.applicability: Any golden or snapshot test whose expected artifact can grow large, especially when multiple normalization layers exist.
relationships: Uses fixture-hygiene-guards for closed inventories and fixed-point scrubbers.
Negative-control-calibration proves the expected output can actually fail.

migration.strategy: Separate compare and refresh into different commands before committing goldens; make CI pass the compare mode explicitly.
migration.implementation: A normalizer with a declared volatile-field list, a compare entry point and a refresh entry point, plus review guidance for diffs.
migration.requiredSupport: Version control review of large expected files and a CI path that cannot request refresh.

positive: Replay compares the live normalized log to the committed file and writes nothing.
Prompt and schema pins produce line-oriented Markdown or structured JSON diffs per composition class.
rejection: Collapsing a dated clock form into the same token as the same-day form fails other scenarios whose goldens deliberately record the dated form.
A missing refresh fails in the PR that changed the web assembly.
recovery: Refresh regenerates sidecars from the normalized live sequence; a following replay proves the working tree stays clean.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes as executed local and CI checks; not re-executed here.

limitations: A normalizer can hide a real difference if it is too broad.
Large goldens still need a review policy; the mechanism does not review itself.
Expected outputs are only as good as the scenario input state; see observation-waits-on-observed-state.

mechanisms.title: Key replay scripts by calling session, harvest every nested log, and cut at an explicit inherited boundary
mechanisms.problem: A single global cursor cannot serve a parent and an in-process child streaming on the same context: it hands the child the parent script. A fork child log also begins with the parent inherited prefix, so deriving from the whole log replays parent responses as child model calls.
triggers: A nested agent, subagent, fork or background child participates in one process.
A new replay scenario has more than one session log.
A recorded child fixture carries a seeded prefix.
obligations: Stamp the calling session id on every model request and route by that id, not by global call order.
Harvest every session log, primary-first, and fail loudly when a live session has no recorded script.
Bind live sessions to recorded scripts by first-call order and advance a cursor per session.
Persist an explicit inherited-prefix boundary at the producer; slice child events at that boundary and never infer it from the current seed length.
Treat a call without a session id as one anonymous session bound to the primary script so the single-session path stays byte-identical.
The inherited boundary is consumed from the persisted fixture's inheritedEventCount, never inferred from the current seed length; child script derivation slices exactly at that boundary.

Live Sessions bind to recorded scripts in first-call order; a session token resolves against actual bound live ids and fails if that Session has not bound; a background child id may be learned from the stable started-subagent tool-result text.
actors: Replay adapter owner: implements keying and fail-loud behavior.
Session/fork backend owner: emits the boundary metadata.
Scenario author: records parent and each child log.
steps: Add the optional session id to the model request options and stamp it from the agent session.
Name fixtures `session[.vN].jsonl` for the parent and `session.<ordinal>[.vN].jsonl` for children; select the highest generation per role.
Sort child fixtures by header `createdAt` and break ties by recorded id.
At live replay, let the first live session to call claim the first script, and so on; error if live sessions exceed recorded scripts.
For fork children, derive the script from events at or after `inheritedEventCount` and mark the boundary in persisted JSONL.

enforcement.mode: runtime routing invariant plus fail-loud error
enforcement.implementation: `GenerateOptions.sessionId`, per-session cursors, `harvestSessionLogs` with primary-first ordering, `inheritEventCount` persisted through `session/end-seed { inherited: true }`, and `fixture.events.slice(inheritedEventCount)`.
enforcement.trust: The producer owns the boundary; the replay harness does not re-derive it from heuristics.
enforcement.failure: More distinct live sessions than recorded scripts is a fail-loud error, never a silent mis-route. A missing session id falls back to the primary script only for the anonymous single-session path.
exceptions: Concurrent or background children must introduce an explicit first-call ordinal instead of relying on timestamps.
An id rename in a config overlay is a review-visible config-rot case, not a wrong snapshot.

mechanisms.applicability: Any replay or record system that can host more than one logical conversation in one process.
relationships: Depends on the fork producer persisting the boundary.

migration.strategy: Add per-caller identity to the request contract before nested scenarios are attempted; make missing routing an error.
migration.implementation: Optional session id on model requests, fixture naming and ordering rules, per-session cursors, explicit boundary metadata and slice.
migration.requiredSupport: A branding-safe id type that does not create an import cycle, and a persistence format that can carry the boundary.

positive: A spawn plus fork mixed scenario routes both children and both branches of the slice.
The single-session path is byte-for-byte unchanged.
rejection: Removing `slice(seedLength)` or the inherited-count slice makes both fork scenarios red because the child receives parent chunks.
A live session with no recorded script fails loudly instead of consuming another script.
recovery: Re-record all fork and spawn fixtures from the real API; keyless runs then reproduce them.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes including a red-to-green check; not re-executed here.

limitations: First-call order assumes siblings run sequentially; concurrent children need an explicit ordinal.
Out-of-process ACP subagents are a different replay shape and remain deferred.
The boundary must be carried through every persistence and restore path or resume can lose it.

mechanisms.title: Derive the test composition from the shipping composition by overlay, not by a hand-maintained twin
mechanisms.problem: Two hand-maintained configs mirrored entry for entry drift silently. If the snapshot tree diverges from the shipping tree, the snapshot tier exercises a different application and reintroduces the green-units-broken-product gap one level up.
triggers: A test app or benchmark app needs a different adapter, transport or backend than production.
A shipping composition gains a plugin or entry that the test tree must also carry.
A reviewer is maintaining a near-copy of a config file.
obligations: Include the shipping config and patch only the entries that must differ.
Address patched entries by stable id and assert the name so a reused id does not disable the wrong plugin.
Keep recording on the unmodified shipping config and replay on the overlay.
Prove the overlay changes nothing else by replaying all existing scenarios with byte-identical expected outputs.
actors: Config owner: maintains base and overlay.
Test author: records with the base config.
Reviewer: checks that the overlay delta stays minimal.
steps: Write `cordis.snapshot.yml` as an include of `cordis.yml`.
Disable the production model adapter by id and name.
Insert the replay adapter.
Permit the intentionally disabled entry in the load guard.
Replay every scenario and confirm expected outputs are unchanged.

enforcement.implementation: Include overlay with `patches`, id plus name targeting, and a load guard that permits the deliberately disabled entry.
enforcement.trust: The base config is the single source; the overlay is a declarative delta.
enforcement.failure: If the id is renamed, the patch degrades to a skip and an extra keyless adapter entry appears. Replay output can still be correct because the replay adapter owns the stream short-circuit, so this is config rot for review, not a wrong snapshot.
exceptions: The overlay relies on patches being applied at include load and not on a later refresh path; it is suitable for a one-shot replay boot with no HMR.
A second divergence is one more patch line, not a second file.

mechanisms.applicability: Test, benchmark and demo compositions that must stay shape-identical to a shipping application.
relationships: Interacts with fixture-hygiene-guards because an overlay can silently add an unloaded entry.

migration.strategy: Replace copies with an overlay that includes the real file; keep the delta declarative and next to the base.
migration.implementation: A loader that applies include patches, stable entry ids, a name assertion on disable patches, and a load guard exception list.
migration.requiredSupport: Config loader with include and patch semantics; review discipline for id stability.

positive: All scenarios pass unchanged on the overlay with byte-identical expected outputs.
rejection: An entry added to the base config appears in the replay tree without a second edit.
A disable patch that targets the wrong name is caught by the name assertion.
recovery: Fix the id or patch target; no fixture regeneration is required if the delta remains one backend swap.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Depends on loader patch semantics and stable ids.
An id rename can leave a futile duplicate entry that does not fail replay; review must catch it.
Not a substitute for a full config test when the overlay itself gains logic.

mechanisms.title: Project the semantic final state of a terminal or renderer instead of pinning raw write fragments or raster images
mechanisms.problem: A stateful renderer depends on ANSI parsing, differential frames, wrapping, scrollback, viewport, width, focus, cursor and presentation intent. Write-fragment tests cannot prove the final screen; the same screen can be produced by different fragments; component-line snapshots miss ANSI effects; raster screenshots include unrelated host rendering noise.
triggers: A terminal or rich renderer has user-visible output not captured by completed event logs.
A transient state such as streaming, pending tools, overlays, reflow, resize or shutdown must be pinned.
A reviewer cannot read the current snapshot format.
obligations: Feed real ANSI writes into a real headless terminal parser and read the final state after synchronized frames quiesce.
Project dimensions, active buffer and viewport coordinates, lifecycle and cursor state, rows, wrap markers and non-default style ranges into text; keep text and style separate.
Freeze animation intervals but allow real elapsed time across one animation tick so the semantic status, not a scheduler-chosen glyph, is pinned.
Enforce theme independence: no RGB colors, no palette entries beyond ANSI 0-15, no explicit background colors; reverse video for selection is allowed.
Own a closed inventory that rejects missing scenarios, missing checkpoints and orphaned expected files.
State which layers the package owns and which the deployment owns (product journeys, PTY smoke).
actors: Package test owner: maintains emulator harness and projection.
Reviewer: reads cell and style diffs.
Deployment owner: owns PTY smoke and assembled product coverage.
steps: Implement a headless terminal against the same terminal interface as production.
Drive production composition and collect ANSI writes.
Wait for synchronized frames to quiesce.
Read the semantic projection and write the expected text.
Run the closed-inventory guard.
On an xterm upgrade, re-run and review the projection.

enforcement.implementation: `HeadlessTerminal` over pinned `@xterm/headless`, frame quiescence, projection fields, theme assertions, closed inventories.
enforcement.trust: The emulator is trusted for terminal parsing; the projection is the reviewable contract.
enforcement.failure: A presentation regression produces a cell/style diff. A missing checkpoint or orphan expected file fails the inventory guard. A theme violation fails the checkpoint.
exceptions: Transient states may be authored directly because a completed session log cannot retain them.
Completed application flows must not be hand-authored; they belong to an assembled deployment test.
PTY tests keep the real loader/input/teardown boundary but do not replace broad state coverage.

mechanisms.applicability: Terminal UIs and other stateful renderers with an emulator or semantic accessibility tree that can expose final state.
relationships: Complements model-visible-surface-snapshot for the model-facing projection.

migration.strategy: Adopt an emulator and a semantic projection before committing terminal goldens; define ownership boundaries early.
migration.implementation: Headless terminal adapter, quiescence wait, projection serializer, theme assertions, inventory check.
migration.requiredSupport: A pinned parser version and a review process for projection changes.

positive: TUI event mapping or presentation regressions produce readable cell and style diffs.
Every checkpoint passes the theme independence rule.
rejection: Raw write fragments change under differential rendering while the screen stays the same, so pinning them would produce false regressions.
A raster screenshot would vary with host fonts and themes.
recovery: Intentional layout changes update and review the package semantic snapshots.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Uses xterm proposed buffer APIs; upgrades require re-review.
Terminal-specific behavior still needs a deployment-owned PTY smoke.
Fixed sizes intentionally encode wrapping and viewport behavior.

mechanisms.title: Snapshot the exact model-visible request surface, not just tool execution
mechanisms.problem: Functional tool assertions prove that a tool ran, but not that the advertised tool schemas, the added system section, or the injected user context reached the model. Tokenizing only a system prompt or tool name can miss the composed request that the model actually sees.
triggers: A profile or runtime changes the model-visible prompt, tool catalog or injected context.
A tool executes correctly but the model may not have been told about it.
A cross-runtime parity claim is being made.
obligations: Record, for every model request, the advertised tool schemas verbatim and the message list in order.
Keep full text for system and user messages, tokenizing only volatile paths; keep only call identity for assistant and tool messages whose text differs by platform.
Omit dynamic runtime context from the recorded profile so every emitted message can be compared.
Use the snapshot, not an inline mock assertion, as the owner of the composed tools and system prompt.
Compare the complete directory and file set, not a cherry-picked subset.
actors: Runtime/profile owner: defines the model-visible surface.
Test author: records the surface and reviews the diff.
Reviewer: checks that the request is the shipped one.
steps: Boot the shipped profile.
Capture each model request: tool schemas verbatim and the ordered message list.
Normalize volatile paths and omit dynamic runtime context.
Write `minimal/model-visible.json`.
Compare the complete set on replay and report a full diff.

enforcement.implementation: A `minimal/model-visible.json` artifact per scenario, with verbatim schema sequences and ordered messages.
enforcement.trust: The recorded request is the model-visible contract.
enforcement.failure: A changed schema, prompt or injected context produces a structured diff. A missing or extra message fails comparison.
exceptions: Assistant and tool text is reduced to call identity because platform-specific rendering differs.
A scenario that deliberately varies dynamic context must not use the minimal profile.

mechanisms.applicability: Agent runtimes and SDKs where the request surface is the product contract and multiple runtimes must agree.
relationships: Complements semantic-state-projection for the human-facing surface.
Supports coverage-plane-honesty when a runtime claims parity.

migration.strategy: Add a minimal profile that suppresses dynamic context, then record the full request surface.
migration.implementation: Request-capture hook, ordered message list, verbatim tool schemas, path tokens, full-set comparison.
migration.requiredSupport: A model adapter or proxy that can capture requests without changing them.

positive: The composed system prompt and tool catalog are visible in one reviewable artifact.
A changed schema appears as a structured diff.
rejection: A tool executing correctly while absent from the advertised schemas fails the snapshot.
A cherry-picked subset would miss an added or removed message.
recovery: Refresh the minimal artifact after an intentional profile change and review the full diff.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: The minimal profile deliberately omits dynamic context, so it does not prove runtime-context injection.
Platform-specific assistant and tool text is not compared.
The artifact is only as complete as the capture point.

mechanisms.title: Make redaction an idempotent fixed point enforced on disk
mechanisms.problem: Large prompts and schemas duplicated in every JSONL fixture turn one edit into dozens of giant one-line diff records, while hand-scrubbing leaves stale review artifacts or reintroduces the content on the next record.
triggers: A fixture stores bytes that are large, duplicated across scenarios, or not behaviorally meaningful.
A normalizer is added to replace volatile or bulky content with tokens.
A record or refresh path can write fixtures.
obligations: Define pure scrubbers for each content class and make every stored file a fixed point of the applicable scrubber.
Tokenize the bulky content in session files and regenerate the authoritative sidecars from the normalized live sequence on every record or refresh.
Keep request-header count, field presence, config, reason and prefix message count; remove only the large content.
Guard uniformity across scenarios in the same composition class so one split pin remains authoritative.
Make required-file symmetry and orphan checks reject stale sidecars.
actors: Fixture owner: defines scrubbers and sidecars.
Record/refresh path: applies scrubbing before writing.
Reviewer: reviews the split Markdown or JSON diff.
steps: Classify the content to tokenize (system prompt, tool schemas, session prefix).
Implement pure scrubbers and a combined scrubber.
Store `{{system}}` and `{{tools}}` tokens in every JSONL.
Regenerate sidecars from the normalized live header sequence.
Enforce each `session*.jsonl` is a fixed point; only non-pinned fixtures must be full-header fixed points.
Run orphan and required-file guards.

enforcement.implementation: Pure scrubbers, tokens such as `"{{system}}"` and `"{{tools}}"`, regenerated sidecars, fixed-point checks and file-symmetry guards.
enforcement.trust: The scrubber is trusted only for the declared content class; the guard proves the stored file has no untokenized copy.
enforcement.failure: A stale duplicate or untokenized prompt fails the fixed-point check. A record path that bypasses scrubbing reintroduces the bulk and fails on the next check.
exceptions: The live product log must remain byte-exact for reconstructability; only test artifacts are scrubbed.
A genuinely distinct composition class gets its own pin; identical classes are caught by the uniformity guard.

mechanisms.applicability: Snapshot corpora with large repeated payloads, secrets, host paths or other non-behavioral bytes that must not dominate review.
relationships: Requires the record path and the compare path to share the normalizer.

migration.strategy: Introduce pure scrubbers and committed sidecars together; never hand-edit the tokenized content.
migration.implementation: Scrub functions, sidecar generators, fixed-point assertions and closed-inventory checks.
migration.requiredSupport: A normalization layer shared by record, refresh and compare.

positive: A system-prompt change produces one line-oriented Markdown diff per composition class.
Every session file is a fixed point of its scrubber.
rejection: A stale `session.expected.jsonl`-style duplicate or an untokenized header fails the fixed-point or orphan guard.
recovery: Re-record or refresh regenerates both the JSONL and the sidecars from the live header sequence.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: A scrubber that is too broad can hide a behaviorally meaningful difference.
Tokenization changes the fixture away from byte-valid production format; consumers must use the matching parser.
The guard proves the declared fixed point, not the semantic completeness of the scrubber.

mechanisms.title: Guard fixture sets as closed inventories and project non-behavioral fields out of review diffs
mechanisms.problem: A snapshot corpus with hand-managed files accumulates orphans, missing required files, duplicated pins and envelope churn. A scenario can pass while its required sidecars are stale or missing, and an insertion can rewrite every later record because volatile sequence and time fields are copied into the golden.
triggers: A snapshot suite has more than one file per scenario.
A fixture format carries sequence numbers, timestamps or other non-behavioral envelope fields.
A new scenario is added or an old one is removed.
obligations: Own a closed inventory per suite: reject missing scenarios, missing checkpoints, missing required files and orphaned expected outputs.
Enforce required-file symmetry for each scenario type; an override sidecar and a session log must not be mutually inconsistent.
Enforce pin uniformity: exactly one pinned scenario per composition class, and every non-pinned fixture must be a fixed point of the full scrubber.
Project non-behavioral envelope fields (`seq`, `time`, `seq0`, `time0`) out of committed snapshots while retaining every payload and top-level discriminative field.
Keep the replay parser able to read the projected form and assign sequence numbers when decoding; keep the runtime persistence format unchanged.
Regenerate required files and sidecars on record or refresh rather than editing them by hand.
actors: Fixture owner: defines the required-file table and inventory.
Snapshot writer: applies projection and scrubbing at its own file boundary.
Replay parser owner: accepts the projected form.
Reviewer: reads the reduced diff.
steps: Write the per-scenario required-file table, including optional override files.
Serialize each record while omitting the projected envelope keys.
Read snapshots back through the projection-aware parser.
Run orphan, missing-file and symmetry checks in the suite meta-test.
Run the one-pin-per-class and fixed-point checks.
On migration, rewrite committed fixtures through the projection so old recording cannot reintroduce the fields.

enforcement.implementation: Closed inventories, required-file symmetry, single-pin checks, scrubber fixed-point assertions, envelope projection in the snapshot writer and compensation in `parseSessionLog`.
enforcement.trust: The inventory and fixed-point checks are mechanical; the projection is trusted only for the declared non-behavioral keys.
enforcement.failure: An orphan, missing file, duplicate pin or untokenized header fails the meta-test. A stale sidecar is rejected rather than silently ignored.
exceptions: Nested payload fields with the same names as projected envelope keys stay unchanged.
The first `session` header is not projected; only body records lose the volatile keys.
A scenario that deliberately records a stateful or dated form keeps it; do not collapse it.

mechanisms.applicability: Snapshot corpora with multiple artifacts per scenario, especially where large or repetitive records would otherwise dominate review.
relationships: Protects record-once-replay-corpus from stale or orphaned fixtures.
Complements replay-script-keying for nested log sets.

migration.strategy: Introduce the inventory and the projection together; migrate all writers and the parser in one cutover.
migration.implementation: A required-file table, meta-tests, scrubber fixed-point checks, writer-side projection and parser-side sequence assignment.
migration.requiredSupport: A shared session-log format catalog so replay and persistence agree on the projected representation.

positive: The repository fixture-layout check uses the replay parser and keeps canonical packed rows.
New events no longer rewrite every later snapshot envelope.
rejection: A duplicate pin, missing required file or orphan expected output is rejected.
A stale repeated expected-log artifact is rejected after the one-artifact decision.
recovery: Re-record or refresh regenerates the files; the migration path rewrites committed fixtures through the projection.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: The guard proves the declared file set and fixed points, not semantic correctness.
Projected files are not byte-valid production logs; every consumer must use the matching parser.
A projection rule per event type would be costly; the source keeps payload references untouched instead.

mechanisms.title: Drive the assembled browser application with replayed model output and normalized semantic goldens
mechanisms.problem: A browser UI can be tested against a standalone client fixture with no real Host, wire or loop, or against a live keyed service. The first cannot catch assembly regressions; the second cannot run on every PR and is nondeterministic.
triggers: A web or desktop client must be covered end to end without a live model key.
A change touches client plugin bundles, the Host wire or the rendered tree.
A platform-specific input behavior needs a second engine.
obligations: Boot the shipped composition through its real config loader, with only the model adapter replayed.
Drive a real browser against the real Host over HTTP JSON-RPC and SSE; do not substitute a hand-built client stand-in for the assembled path.
Capture the semantic UI surface (for example the aria tree), normalize volatile values, and compare against committed expected outputs.
Keep browser-driving code outside per-file coverage gates that cannot honestly measure it; put gate-worthy logic in gated packages.
Run the full suite in the primary engine and a narrow subset in a second engine only for behavior that engine uniquely exercises.
Run HMR or other state-mutating scenarios outside the parallel pool.

Treat only the Host's idle signal, which follows the persistence flush, plus a settled semantic surface as turn completion; a bare turn/end event, persistence-file polling, or networkidle is not a completion barrier.
Fail on any page error or connection-loss/gap-repair console warning, and assert at teardown that every recorded script and cursor was consumed.
Do not retry the lane; isolate each scenario with one browser and host, a fresh context, a pinned viewport, semantic selectors, and an explicit locale.

An assembled Web lane must own a fully hermetic world (temporary workspace, persistence, harness home, agents and bundled-skill roots, storage root), mask and restore ambient credentials, disable ambient telemetry, and authenticate through the real token exchange; ambient home and skill roots must not leak into replay requests.

Only explicit refresh writes goldens; a missing golden fails with the regeneration command. Console connection-loss/gap-repair warnings and page errors fail the scenario; only connection-loss warnings after an intentional reload may be acknowledged, gap-repair warnings remain fatal.

Aria goldens normalize volatile values but preserve literal relative age unless the region explicitly opts in; capture waits for two consecutive equal normalized captures and restores expanded controls in finally.
actors: Web lane owner: maintains scaffold, fixtures and normalizer.
Scenario author: records and reviews goldens.
CI: runs replay-only with an explicit worker budget.
steps: Load the shipping web config and patch test-only roots, disabled watchers and persistence paths.
Serve the built client and Host.
Replay the recorded model script and drive the page.
Wait for the semantic surface to stabilize.
Normalize and compare to the committed golden.
Run state-mutating scenarios serially and the rest in one bounded pool.

enforcement.implementation: `test:web` and `test:web:ci` with `DSH_SNAPSHOT=replay`, `launchWebScaffold`, normalized aria goldens, separate HMR run, worker budget via `DSH_WEB_SNAPSHOT_WORKERS`.
enforcement.trust: The assembled browser and Host are production; only the model is replayed.
enforcement.failure: A semantic mismatch fails the file. A missing golden refresh fails the PR. A worker-budget change requires an end-to-end measurement.
exceptions: A second engine is used only for behavior the primary engine cannot exercise.
A server-only or pure unit concern belongs in a lower layer.

mechanisms.applicability: Web, Electron or desktop clients that compose many bundles and a Host process and whose user-visible contract is a semantic tree.
relationships: Shared prerequisite: no-false-green-preflight for the keyless lane.

migration.strategy: Start from the shipped config, add the replay adapter, and capture the semantic tree rather than pixels or DOM internals.
migration.implementation: Browser scaffold, config patches, aria normalizer, golden files, CI gate registration.
migration.requiredSupport: A browser automation runtime, a stable semantic surface and a build artifact the lane can serve.

positive: A keyless replay exercises Chromium through the real wire and renders the committed semantic tree.
The second engine covers the input behavior it uniquely owns.
rejection: A standalone client fixture would pass while the Host wire is broken.
A jsdom snapshot cannot cover HTTP/SSE carriage or real plugin bundle composition.
recovery: Refresh the goldens after an intentional UI change and review the churn; replay again.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: The lane makes no cross-platform browser consistency claim.
A browser or automation upgrade that changes the semantic format requires an explicit refresh and review.
Worker-budget changes need a completed measurement.
First-call-order replay binding limits a scenario to one prompting session; shared replay cursors stay inert only under the published catalog window.

mechanisms.title: Exercise the installed artifact through its public entry point, not the source tree
mechanisms.problem: A unit suite can drive fake peers and pass while the packaged artifact is broken. Checking out the repo, installing editable, or importing from source hides a mismatched SDK and runtime, a broken native wheel, a missing platform closure or a failure in the real entry point.
triggers: A package is shipped as a wheel, binary, installer or bundle.
A PR could break packaging or native dependencies while source tests stay green.
A runtime and SDK version must agree at the installed boundary.
obligations: Build the distributable artifacts before the behavior test.
Install the built artifacts into a clean environment, change directory outside the repository, and unset source-resolution variables such as `PYTHONPATH` and runtime-mode overrides.
Invoke only public modules and the packaged executable.
Reject a non-clean environment, a repository-relative working directory, a source or editable import, and unequal SDK/runtime versions.
Run the installed-artifact gate as a required PR check on the platforms claimed.
actors: Packaging owner: produces the wheel or installer.
CI: creates the clean environment and runs the black-box checks.
Reviewer: verifies the platform matrix.
steps: Build the SDK and each runtime distribution.
Create a fresh virtual environment for each native target.
Install the two local files.
Move outside the repository and clear source-resolution variables.
Import public modules and run the packaged executable.
Assert version agreement and reject any source import.

enforcement.implementation: A build-then-install job with a black-box harness that asserts environment cleanliness, cwd, import origin and version equality.
enforcement.trust: The installed artifact is the product under test.
enforcement.failure: A source import, editable install, repository cwd or version mismatch fails the gate. A missing platform artifact fails the matrix.
exceptions: The default development suite may still use source imports for fast feedback; it cannot substitute for the installed gate.
A platform with no distributable yet must not be silently claimed as covered.

mechanisms.applicability: Any project that ships an installable or native artifact and whose source tests can mask packaging failures.
relationships: Extends record-once-replay-corpus to the artifact boundary.
Installed-artifact-qualification adds update and install-state coverage.

migration.strategy: Add the build-then-install job before claiming PR coverage; keep source tests as fast feedback.
migration.implementation: Wheel or bundle build, clean venv or container, public-entry smoke, environment assertions.
migration.requiredSupport: A CI matrix for each advertised platform and a packaging step that runs before behavior tests.

positive: A clean environment imports the installed SDK and runs the packaged executable against the installed runtime.
Each native target installs the two local artifacts and passes.
rejection: A source or editable import is rejected.
A mismatched SDK/runtime version or broken native wheel fails before merge.
recovery: Rebuild and reinstall after fixing packaging; the gate reruns from a clean environment.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: The gate covers the platforms and entry points it actually invokes.
A clean environment does not prove every optional integration.
Cost grows with the platform matrix.

mechanisms.title: Qualify the installed/update lifecycle with real artifacts, retained test-only identities, and fail-closed receipts
mechanisms.problem: A successful file copy does not prove a signed installer exists or that the installed application will start. Normal release paths expose test metadata, and an installed-update walkthrough needs two increasing versions with a shared identity. Simulated update events cannot establish feed parsing, integrity, download and platform preparation together.
triggers: An updater, installer or packaged desktop application must be verified.
A test needs two versions of an installed application.
A qualification run must not depend on production release infrastructure.
obligations: Prepare test-only versions from a retained manifest with a random identity and distribution namespace; change only release-family versions and matching dependencies.
Seal and verify inventories, re-verify the source, and refuse to overwrite existing outputs.
Generate a bootstrap that validates installed package identity before importing production main.
Run the production update coordinator inside the real runtime with a real HTTP executor and updater, against a loopback feed served by an isolated server.
Allocate a fresh temporary directory and an OS-assigned port per invocation; use request barriers and observations instead of sleeps.
Keep signature or publisher verification absent only in the private fixture configuration, never in production.
A failed copy retains a failure record and cannot create a completion receipt.
actors: Release/qualification engineer: prepares materials and runs the harness.
Update owner: owns the production coordinator and feed format.
CI or local operator: runs the isolated qualification.
steps: Build two increasing versions with a shared app identity.
Seal inventories and verify the source descriptor hash.
Install version one into an isolated directory.
Serve a loopback update feed with the intended policy.
Drive the production update coordinator and observe download, integrity, preparation and restart behavior.
Assert the post-update identity and retain the journal or failure record.

enforcement.implementation: Material preparer with manifests and inventory seals, generated bootstrap identity check, real updater plus loopback feed, atomic temp and port allocation, observations replacing UI interaction, journal and receipt rules.
enforcement.trust: The production coordinator and installer preparation path are real; only the feed and UI observations are controlled.
enforcement.failure: A copy without a signed installer, an identity mismatch, a missing inventory entry or a failed update step must fail and leave a record rather than a success receipt.
exceptions: Publisher verification may be absent only in the private fixture configuration.
The test manifest is retained test-only metadata and must not leak into production release paths.

mechanisms.applicability: Desktop applications, installers and updaters whose correctness depends on the installed state and the updater lifecycle.
relationships: Uses fault-injection-and-recovery for feed and network failures.
Uses evidence-scoped-claims to avoid extrapolating from one platform.

migration.strategy: Build the real artifact pair and an isolated feed before writing update assertions; make success require a verified receipt.
migration.implementation: Test-only manifests, sealed inventories, generated bootstrap, loopback feed, atomic allocation and journal.
migration.requiredSupport: A platform installer toolchain and a runtime that can host the production updater.

positive: The installed application starts, updates from the loopback feed and preserves its identity.
The journal records the update and the receipt matches the installed state.
rejection: A successful copy without a signed installer fails qualification.
An identity mismatch in the generated bootstrap is rejected before production main runs.
recovery: A failed copy retains its failure record and cannot produce a completion receipt; rerun in a fresh directory and port.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: The source notes describe Windows qualification and local updater paths; other platforms need their own evidence.
A private fixture may omit publisher verification and therefore does not prove production signing.
The harness is heavy and local-first; it is not a cheap per-PR unit test.

mechanisms.title: Test the real boot and mount path instead of a hand-built bench or a programmable remote fake
mechanisms.problem: A hand-built bench with a bare context, stand-ins and slot declarations asserts the bench, not the product. A programmable remote fake reimplements Gateway semantics and can permit behaviors the real system forbids, such as a unary rejection.
triggers: A client or plugin host has a production boot and mount path.
A test constructs a context, remote or transport by hand.
A fake transport accepts a call shape the real protocol rejects.
obligations: Boot the real client assembly with its production config and include rules.
Use a remote mock that answers by endpoint name and shares the real protocol contract, rather than a programmable fake that can invent semantics.
Read the plugin roster from the bundles, including inject and immediately metadata, rather than listing plugins in the test.
Keep the assembly tier in a test-runtime package that does not import the Host or dynamically import product code.
Assert the same closure and selection behavior the product performs.
actors: Client assembly owner: maintains boot and mount.
Test-runtime owner: provides the real assembly and endpoint-named remote mock.
Scenario author: drives the assembled client.
steps: Build the production boot path with one connection.
Load the plugin roster from bundle entries.
Filter to the platform and carry inject metadata.
Mount the client.
Answer remote calls by endpoint name with contract-shaped responses.
Assert user-visible behavior through the assembled tree.

enforcement.implementation: `dsh-client-test-runtime` assembly tier and `dsh-remote-mock` endpoint-name responses; no Host import and no dynamic import.
enforcement.trust: The real boot and mount path are the system under test; the remote boundary is contract-shaped.
enforcement.failure: A hand-built bench can stay green while the real assembly is broken. A programmable fake can allow an impossible call and hide a protocol regression.
exceptions: Pure helpers may still be unit-tested directly.
A transport fault may be injected at the narrow writer boundary, but the connection contract remains real.

mechanisms.applicability: Clients, plugin hosts and other composed systems with a production boot path and a remote or plugin boundary.
relationships: Supports coverage-plane-honesty because the real assembly is what coverage claims apply to.

migration.strategy: Move from hand-built benches to the production boot path; keep the remote mock contract-shaped.
migration.implementation: A test runtime that exposes production assembly, bundle-derived rosters and an endpoint-named remote mock.
migration.requiredSupport: A boot path that can run under test without the Host, and a protocol schema the mock can follow.

positive: A focused source test boots the real client assembly and mounts it.
Plugin roster and inject metadata come from the bundles.
rejection: A programmable fake that permits a unary rejection would pass tests the real Gateway would fail.
A hand-built context would not catch a boot or mount regression.
recovery: Use the assembly tier for the failing path and add the missing contract to the endpoint-named mock.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: The assembly tier itself must be maintained as a real product path, not a second implementation.
An endpoint-named mock still needs contract coverage for each answer shape.
A test that cannot import the Host may need a different boundary for Host-side behavior.

mechanisms.title: Mock only the external boundary; never reimplement the contract inside the test
mechanisms.problem: A test double that reimplements protocol semantics can accept states the real system forbids and hides whether the boundary preserved distinctions. In-process adapter mocks also bypass fetch, HTTP parsing, SSE framing, socket termination and idle watchdogs.
triggers: A test needs to control a network peer, model adapter or process boundary.
A mock has begun parsing, framing, sequencing or retrying on behalf of the product.
A fault distinction such as reset-before-first-event versus clean EOF matters.
obligations: Place the double at the narrowest external boundary (socket, HTTP server, model stream or message writer).
Keep the shipping adapter, loop, retry policy, framing and parsing in the test path.
Preserve distinct fault classes rather than collapsing them into one generic failure.
Inject transport failure through the real writer callback contract, not by reaching into host-specific pipe internals.
Make the double report facts, not retryability or policy decisions.
actors: Test-infrastructure owner: provides the boundary double.
Adapter or connection owner: defines the real contract and fault classes.
Scenario author: chooses the narrowest sufficient boundary.
steps: Identify the external boundary the product actually consumes.
Implement the double at that boundary with explicit behaviors.
Drive the real adapter and loop through it.
Assert request counts, body identity and recovery behavior.
Keep impossible states impossible in the double unless a script explicitly requests them.

enforcement.implementation: A scriptable wire-fault server, a message-writer injection hook, an endpoint-named remote mock, and a real child process kept alive behind a controlled writer.
enforcement.trust: The product boundary is real; only the external peer is controlled.
enforcement.failure: A generic mock failure hides whether failed chunks stayed outside committed model history. A fake that permits an impossible call hides a contract regression.
exceptions: A pure unit test may mock an internal seam for speed, but it cannot substitute for the boundary test.
A scripted server can share an arrival-ordered script across clients; that limitation must be stated.

mechanisms.applicability: Adapters, transports, RPC clients, subprocess plumbing and any layer with a documented external protocol.
relationships: Depends on evidence-scoped-claims for what the double actually proves.

migration.strategy: Replace contract-reimplementing fakes with a boundary server or writer hook; keep fault classes explicit.
migration.implementation: A scriptable HTTP/SSE server, a writer injection hook, an endpoint-named remote mock.
migration.requiredSupport: A stable external protocol and a way to run the shipping adapter against a local peer.

positive: The real HTTP/SSE adapter, loop and retry policy run against scripted faults; request counts and retry steps match.
A transport write failure is distinguished from process exit without platform pipe internals.
rejection: An in-process adapter mock bypasses fetch, status parsing and SSE framing, so it cannot catch those regressions.
A programmable remote fake that allows a unary rejection would pass where the real Gateway fails.
recovery: Add the missing behavior or fault class to the boundary double; do not move it into product code.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A boundary double still needs its own tests.
Arrival-ordered shared scripts can make concurrency tests ambiguous.
The double does not prove remote production behavior, only the contract it models.

mechanisms.title: Use one owned subprocess primitive for spawn, collection, timeout and termination
mechanisms.problem: Dozens of tests re-derived spawn, stdout collection, timeout, SIGKILL and exit settlement by hand. Variations silently changed settlement order and leaked children, and hand-tokenized CLI flags duplicated a standard parser.
triggers: A test or helper spawns a child process.
A suite needs captured output, a timeout or a kill path.
A CLI fixture parses flags or env files.
obligations: Use a single shared subprocess helper for spawn, output collection, timeout and termination instead of per-file implementations.
Make settlement explicit: one exit or error, bounded wait, then a kill path.
Dispose children on timeout and on test failure; do not leave orphans.
Use the runtime standard parser and env loader instead of hand-rolled tokenization.
Keep the real child alive when the test is about the parent transport contract, and inject failure at the writer.
actors: Test-infrastructure owner: maintains the helper.
Scenario author: consumes it.
CI: relies on bounded teardown.
steps: Call the shared spawn helper with the command and timeout.
Collect stdout and stderr with a bounded buffer.
Wait for exit with a single settlement.
On timeout, terminate the tree and surface the failure.
Assert the collected output or exit status.

enforcement.implementation: One subprocess utility replacing hand-rolled spawn, timeout and SIGKILL code; standard `parseArgs` and env loader.
enforcement.trust: The helper owns process lifetime; tests do not reimplement it.
enforcement.failure: A timeout that does not kill leaves a leaked child and contaminates later tests. A hand-rolled settlement can report success before the child exits.
exceptions: A test of process lifetime itself may need direct control; it must still restore and dispose.
A PTY harness may wrap the helper but keeps the same settlement rules.

mechanisms.applicability: Every test suite that spawns binaries, language runtimes or Git.

migration.strategy: Consolidate on the standard runtime APIs and one helper before raising timeouts.
migration.implementation: A helper around the runtime child-process API, standard CLI parsing, and explicit settlement.
migration.requiredSupport: A runtime with reliable child-process semantics and a test cleanup registry.

positive: All spawn sites use one helper and settle once.
Timeout tests terminate the child and leave no process.
rejection: A hand-rolled collector that resolves on stdout close before exit would fail the settlement assertion.
Hand-tokenized flags that disagree with the standard parser are removed.
recovery: On a kill failure, surface it as a teardown failure rather than retrying without ownership.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: A shared helper can grow options; keep the contract narrow.
Platform-specific tree kill still needs its own evidence.
The helper does not make an unbounded child safe; the caller must set a budget.

mechanisms.title: Model concurrent host resources and give every test its own namespace, cleanup owner and environment
mechanisms.problem: Concurrent Vitest files, workers, gates and jobs share ports, predictable paths, external namespaces and inherited children. Process isolation does not isolate those resources, so a test can select the right tier and pass alone while failing in CI. Global mutations and incomplete teardown contaminate later tests.
triggers: A test or fixture acquires a host resource (port, path, process, listener, env var, global singleton).
A test can pass alone but fails in the full lane.
A suite is about to use a fixed path, fixed port or process-wide setting.
obligations: Inventory the resources a test owns and the concurrency it can meet (files, workers, gates, jobs, sibling runners).
Allocate unique temporary directories and OS-assigned ports; pair each root with the run result that produced it rather than assuming allocation order.
Set process-wide environment at the runner or workflow boundary, not inside a test; make the setting inherit to child processes deliberately.
Do not mutate process-global state without restoring it, and dispose listeners, watchers, children and directories even when setup fails.
Keep shared caches persistent only when the manager supports concurrent access; state the operational ownership of capacity and residue.
Model external namespaces and inherited children; do not assume process exit closes them.
actors: Test author: declares owned resources and cleanup.
Test-infrastructure owner: provides allocators and guards.
CI operator: owns runner capacity, temp storage and caches.
steps: List the resources and the maximum concurrency.
Replace fixed values with allocated ones.
Register cleanup immediately after successful acquisition.
Restore process-global state in a finally path, including setup failure.
Set lane-scoped environment before any child starts.
Run the suite under the real concurrent topology, not only alone.

enforcement.mode: test design, shared helpers and CI configuration
enforcement.implementation: Unique temp allocators, OS-assigned ports, `TMPDIR=runner.temp` exported through `GITHUB_ENV`, worker-level runtime flags, cleanup registries and disposal assertions.
enforcement.trust: Each test owns only its declared namespace; the runner owns the rest.
enforcement.failure: A fixed path or port can collide across workers. A leaked child or listener contaminates later tests. A shared temp directory can exhaust and fail unrelated PRs before tests execute.
exceptions: A deliberately shared cache may be retained if the package manager supports concurrent access and capacity is owned operationally.
A test of process-global behavior must restore it and must not run concurrently with a test that depends on the default.

mechanisms.applicability: Every parallel test suite and every fixture that touches the host outside the language runtime.
relationships: Used by test-reliability-governance for probabilistic failure diagnosis.

migration.strategy: Inventory resources first, then remove fixed paths, ports and globals; make cleanup registration automatic.
migration.implementation: Allocator helpers, cleanup registry, lane-scoped env, runner-owned temp, concurrency-aware caches.
migration.requiredSupport: CI configuration control, a temp allocator, and a cleanup assertion that runs on failure.

positive: The suite passes under the real multi-worker topology and on a shared-volume runner.
Every acquired directory and child has a single cleanup owner.
rejection: A fixed port or predictable path would collide under concurrency.
A test that mutates a process global without restore contaminates a later test.
recovery: On a collision, allocate a new value; on a leaked resource, surface it as a teardown failure rather than retrying.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: Process isolation still does not isolate host resources; the inventory must be maintained.
A shared cache can fail for capacity or filesystem reasons that tests cannot fix.
The source explicitly leaves historical residue and disk provisioning to operators.

mechanisms.title: Give every fixture an explicit lifetime: acquire, register cleanup, restore on setup failure, and prove disposal
mechanisms.problem: Fixtures that allocate subprocesses, watchers, temp directories or patched methods leak when setup fails or when a timeout fires. A test can report a teardown failure without identifying which resource exceeded its budget, and a requested termination is not proof that disposal finished.
triggers: A fixture spawns a process, opens a watcher or listener, patches a method, or allocates a directory.
A test can time out during setup or teardown.
Cleanup failures appear only on a contended host.
obligations: Register cleanup immediately after successful acquisition, before any assertion that can fail.
Restore patched factories and dispose the context even when setup fails before the local cleanup block.
Make disposal await the actual resource outcome (child exit, watcher closure, directory removal) rather than only requesting termination.
Keep failure cleanup waiting for disposal and child completion before removing the private directory.
A teardown failure must identify the resource and budget; do not mask it with a retry.
Use the lane test or hook budget for the fixture lifetime, not a smaller independent deadline.
actors: Fixture owner: defines acquisition and disposal.
Test author: uses the registration hook.
CI: enforces hook and test budgets.
steps: Acquire the resource and register its cleanup immediately.
Wrap setup in a path that still runs restoration on failure.
On timeout or assertion failure, request termination and await settlement.
Assert the resource is gone before the next case.
Surface any disposal failure with the resource name.

enforcement.implementation: Cleanup registries, factory restoration in a failure path, disposal awaited under the lane budget, deferred exit observation, bounded child kill.
enforcement.trust: The fixture owns the resource until it proves disposal.
enforcement.failure: A requested kill that is not awaited can leave an orphan; a setup-failure path can leak a watcher or factory override; a teardown failure that omits the resource is not diagnosable.
exceptions: A test of teardown latency must assert the contract, not one winner of a race.
A process that needs a real descendant tree kill uses the platform-specific mechanism, and a failed tree kill remains a failure.

mechanisms.applicability: All fixtures that own resources, especially subprocess, watcher and patched-global fixtures.
relationships: Interacts with timeout-budgeting for hook and test deadlines.

migration.strategy: Add a cleanup registry and a setup-failure path before widening budgets; make disposal awaitable.
migration.implementation: A per-test disposal list, factory restore hooks, awaited child exit, and resource-named failures.
migration.requiredSupport: A test runner with teardown hooks and a child-process API that exposes exit.

positive: A forced setup failure still closes the watcher and restores the factory before the next case.
Teardown waits for child completion and then removes the private directory.
rejection: A requested termination alone does not prove disposal; a deferred observation shows the process tree exit.
An unregistered temp directory remains after failure and is caught.
recovery: Retry cleanup only through safe removal within the documented window; a failed tree kill is surfaced, not ignored.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A cleanup assertion can still time out on a severely contended host; raising the hook budget is a separate decision.
Some resources are outside the account ability to remove.
The mechanism does not fix capacity or filesystem failure.

mechanisms.title: Synchronize with explicit barriers and injected clocks instead of sleeps or transient DOM assumptions
mechanisms.problem: Wall-clock sleeps approximate readiness, fake timers can deadlock holds that read time twice, and asserting a transient DOM state before the product has completed its transition produces false failures. None of these establishes the state the test needs.
triggers: A test waits for asynchronous startup, streaming, animation or a background handshake.
A test uses a fixed delay before asserting.
A rendered value is held by a timer or transition.
obligations: Replace sleeps with event-driven waits or an explicit barrier the harness controls.
Inject a clock that advances from a fixed anchor with real elapsed time when product code reads time twice; a permanently frozen clock can prevent a hold from ever elapsing.
Wait for synchronized frames or quiescence before reading a renderer state.
Assert stable semantic states, not intermediate transitions.
Keep the barrier and clock controls in the fixture; do not add scenario-local product overrides that test a page the product does not serve.
actors: Fixture author: provides barriers and clock injection.
Scenario author: asserts only after the barrier.
Reviewer: rejects sleep-based synchronization.
steps: Identify the real completion signal for the operation.
Expose a barrier or an awaited event in the fixture.
If time itself is under test, inject a clock; otherwise wait on events.
Read the state after quiescence.
Remove fixed settling delays.

enforcement.implementation: Event-driven waits, barrier toggles, `pinHostClock`/`pinBrowserClock`, frame quiescence, semantic-state assertions.
enforcement.trust: The barrier or observed event owns readiness; elapsed time does not.
enforcement.failure: A sleep can pass on a fast host and fail on a slow one. A frozen clock can strand a two-reading hold. A transient assertion can capture the wrong state.
exceptions: Fake timers are appropriate when the timer service itself is under test.
A deliberately dated or stateful rendering is a real assertion; do not collapse it in normalization.

mechanisms.applicability: UI tests, streaming tests, and any test with asynchronous startup or animations.
relationships: Used by replay-assembled-lane and web scenario tests.
Supports timeout-budgeting by removing delay-based races.

migration.strategy: Replace sleeps with explicit barriers; add clock injection only where hold semantics are tested.
migration.implementation: Barrier primitives, clock spies with anchor and elapsed time, frame-quiescence waits.
migration.requiredSupport: A fixture surface that can control the page or process without changing product behavior.

positive: A scenario renders the same semantic state regardless of host speed.
A two-reading hold still elapses because the clock advances with real time.
rejection: A permanently frozen browser clock leaves settled text unrendered.
A fixed delay captures a transition and fails on a loaded host.
recovery: Add the missing barrier or observation and rerun; do not raise the delay.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes including a measured 10/61 failure without the observation and 20/20 with it; not re-executed here.

limitations: A barrier that the product does not expose may require a controlled test seam.
Clock injection can change timing-sensitive behavior; prefer event waits where possible.
Quiescence does not prove semantic correctness by itself.

mechanisms.title: Establish the input state and observe the completion the assertion needs; a timeout is a budget, not delivery evidence
mechanisms.problem: A capture can land on a different state than the golden records when the state is implied by pointer position, keyboard modality or an in-flight host read. A wait can stop after two equal snapshots that both show the wrong state. An event can be missed entirely and no deadline can recover it.
triggers: A golden records a hovered row, focused tooltip, enabled status or other stateful rendering.
A test polls or captures after an action.
An operating-system or browser event may be delayed, coalesced or dropped.
obligations: Before capture, establish the state the golden records: hover the intended row, clear the pointer-input flag, focus the intended control, or wait for the value published by the later read.
Poll the exact observed value until it equals the expected token or state; do not sample once.
Do not rely on a stability heuristic (two equal snapshots) as proof of the correct state.
Make deadlines budgets for bounded work; a deadline cannot recover an event that was never emitted.
When a real event cannot be guaranteed, deliver it through a controlled watcher while a separate owning test covers native delivery.
Separate visual transitions from JavaScript timers; they use different clocks.
actors: Scenario author: names and establishes the input state.
Fixture owner: provides controlled delivery and exact observation helpers.
Reviewer: checks that the assertion owns its precondition.
steps: Write down which state the golden represents.
Perform the input or wait for the exact published value before capture.
Poll computed values to the independent token rather than checking presence.
For native event delivery, use a controlled watcher for semantic tests and keep native delivery in its own test.
Never replace a missing observation with a longer timeout.

enforcement.implementation: Explicit hover/focus setup, polling predicates, `captureStableAria` plus correct-state establishment, controlled Chokidar watcher, independent color-token read.
enforcement.trust: The observed value is the only evidence the state exists.
enforcement.failure: A single sample inside a status-transition window reads the old value. A stable snapshot of the wrong state passes the stability check but fails the golden. A held event can never arrive, so extending the deadline fails too.
exceptions: A real operating-system delivery guarantee belongs to a dedicated native test, not to every semantic assertion.
A timeout test still needs a bounded budget; the budget is not evidence of the event.

mechanisms.applicability: Browser, terminal, HMR and any asynchronous UI scenario whose assertion depends on a state the harness does not otherwise own.
relationships: Related to owned-completion-observation for server-side completion.

migration.strategy: Make each capture name its state and each wait poll the exact value; split native delivery into its own test.
migration.implementation: Polling helpers, controlled watcher injection, independent token reads, explicit focus/hover setup.
migration.requiredSupport: A fixture API that can establish input state and expose the observed value.

positive: The three browser scenarios render the aria their goldens record whatever state the harness arrives in.
The connection test polls computed colors to the independent tokens.
rejection: A bare mouse press without a key raises no tooltip, so the running capture fails with the missing bubble.
A single status read inside the 61ms window captures the pre-reload value.
recovery: Establish the state, poll the value, or control delivery; then rerun.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes with negative controls; not re-executed here.

limitations: Polling can still time out if the product never publishes the value.
A controlled watcher does not test native delivery.
A real visual transition may still be in progress after the token matches; use the computed value, not the intention.

mechanisms.title: Wait on the completion signal that owns the operation, not an earlier acceptance or a bare process start
mechanisms.problem: HTTP acceptance, projected UI state, process startup and durable completion are separate observations. A test that waits one second for a webhook-created session, or five seconds for PowerShell output, measures an unrelated prefix. A 202 response does not prove the session or model request exists.
triggers: An operation crosses an HTTP boundary, a process boundary or a durable log.
A test waits a fixed time after a request.
A teardown must prove disposal rather than a termination request.
obligations: Identify the completion signal that owns the operation (session creation, `turn/end`, child output in scrollback, journal entry, process-tree exit).
Hold the intermediate operation behind a barrier and assert its absence before releasing it.
Await the owning signal, not a wall-clock window.
Release barriers and restore listeners on timeout so cleanup still runs.
For readiness, accept every supported tier and reject timeout or exit settlements that are not readiness.
For teardown, await disposal and child completion; a requested kill is not completion.
actors: Fixture author: exposes the completion signal and barriers.
Test author: asserts only the owning signal.
CI: provides lane budgets for the bounded wait.
steps: Map the operation stages: acceptance, projection, durable completion.
Choose the durable or process signal that proves the assertion.
Hold the pre-completion stage and assert the absence of the later artifact.
Release and await the owning signal.
Clean up in a finally path even on timeout.

enforcement.implementation: Barriers around workspace creation or child startup, awaited `turn/end` or journal entry, deferred exit observation, scrollback observation for shell output.
enforcement.trust: Only the owning signal proves completion; acceptance and startup are prefixes.
enforcement.failure: A one-second poll after HTTP 202 can fail while creation is slow. A process-start marker does not prove the command ran. A termination request does not prove the tree exited.
exceptions: A test of latency itself may measure a prefix, but then it must say so.
A supported inferred-idle readiness tier is acceptable when the protocol defines it; a timeout settlement is not.

mechanisms.applicability: Server-side integration tests, process-lifecycle tests and any test that currently sleeps after a request or a spawn.
relationships: Uses fixture-lifecycle-ownership for cleanup on timeout.

migration.strategy: Replace post-request delays with owning signals and add absence assertions before release.
migration.implementation: Barrier hooks, durable-log queries, journal reads, awaited child exit, scrollback observation.
migration.requiredSupport: A log or API that exposes the completion event and a fixture seam that can hold the intermediate stage.

positive: The GitHub review test holds Workspace creation, proves neither Agent nor model request exists, releases and awaits the matching turn end.
The PowerShell test observes formatted child output in scrollback rather than an echoed command.
rejection: A one-second webhook poll fails on a slow but successful creation.
An echoed output string present in the command text does not prove execution.
recovery: On timeout, release the barrier, restore the method and remove the listener before failing.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A durable signal may not exist for every operation; then the test must state a bounded inference.
A supported readiness tier can be wider than a single exact state.
A true process exit may still leave external side effects outside the test namespace.

mechanisms.title: Let one lane budget govern case and hook time, and delete per-case ceilings that silently undercut it
mechanisms.problem: A describe-level timeout overrides the lane argument, so a smaller per-suite value caps every case even when the lane grants more. Raising only the test budget moves a contended suite failure from the case into teardown because the hook budget remains at the default. Retrying hides the host property that caused the failure.
triggers: A suite is bound by process creation rather than assertions.
A suite has a describe-level timeout or per-case allowances.
A lane grants a test budget but leaves the hook budget at its default.
obligations: Express the budget once for the lane or suite, aligned with the lane environment value.

Delete per-case allowances that merely restate a describe value; a later case without one would silently inherit a different ceiling. When a file runs under lanes whose root config has no raised default (plain test command or a parity lane), an explicit per-case budget aligned with the lane value is acceptable and must be stated.
Set `--hookTimeout` alongside the test and poll timeouts so setup and teardown have the same budget.
Do not shorten a cleanup retry window just to fit a smaller hook budget.
Do not retry a timed-out suite; retrying moves the failure and leaves a red or green gate that carries no code information.
Record the trade-off: a raised ceiling accepts a real slowdown that the old ceiling would have caught; the old ceiling was firing on host contention.
actors: Test owner: chooses the suite budget.
Lane owner: sets the environment value.
CI operator: owns host capacity.
steps: Measure the slowest case on an idle host to understand the headroom.
Align the suite value with the lane test budget.
Remove duplicated per-case constants.
Emit the hook timeout from the same variable.
Run under the contended lane and confirm the failure moves from the budget to real assertions.

enforcement.implementation: `DSH_COVERAGE_TEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, `--testTimeout`, `--expect.poll.timeout`, `--hookTimeout`, suite-level values, deletion of per-case constants.
enforcement.trust: The lane environment owns the host property; suites defer to it.
enforcement.failure: A describe value below the lane cap silently lowers the budget. A missing hook timeout reproduces the failure in teardown. A retry hides a real regression or a real capacity problem.
exceptions: A test of a genuine latency contract may carry a smaller explicit budget and must state why.
Lanes that do not set the variable keep every runtime default.

A spawning file that runs under both a raised lane and a default-config lane may need an explicit per-case budget equal to the lane value; the source did this for the oxlint spawn cases because the root config had no testTimeout. This is not a licence to restate a describe value in a suite that already has one.

mechanisms.applicability: Any multi-tenant CI lane where process creation or host contention, not the assertion, decides timeout outcomes.
relationships: Uses test-isolation-hermeticity for the host property.

migration.strategy: Adopt one lane variable for test and hook budgets; delete per-case restatements.
migration.implementation: Workflow environment, coverage argument builder, suite-level timeout, documented trade-off.
migration.requiredSupport: A workflow parser test or equivalent check that the assignment reaches every worker.

positive: The Windows coverage lane runs the process-bound suites without budget-caused failures.
A slow fixture teardown no longer fails an otherwise passing suite.
rejection: A describe-level 15s value caps all 23 cases while the lane grants 90s.
A raised test budget with the default 10s hook still fails in teardown.
recovery: Raise the lane budget or fix the host; do not retry the suite.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A wider budget accepts a real slowdown into tens of seconds.
It does not make the host faster or fix capacity.
