Cold-start costs may still exceed any reasonable budget and need their own observation.

mechanisms.title: Keep supported-platform tests semantic and exclude only the fixture whose state cannot exist
mechanisms.problem: Literal POSIX paths become drive-relative on Windows, a hosted file URI can be a valid UNC path, child-pipe closure and event-loop scheduling differ, and POSIX-only file states have no direct Windows fixture. Treating fixture syntax as product behavior reports false regressions or encourages production normalization that erases native semantics.
triggers: A test runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
A fixture builds a path, URI or filesystem state by hand.
A platform-specific exclusion is proposed.
obligations: Build absolute paths and file URIs with the host `node:path` and `node:url` APIs; assert native absolute output or stable workspace-relative output as the contract requires.
Use invalid-URI encodings rejected by `fileURLToPath()` on every supported platform.
Inject transport failure through the connection message writer and deliver the same asynchronous callback error a real stream reports.
Implement descendant-tree teardown with a negative process-group id on POSIX and synchronous `taskkill /T /F` on Windows; only suppress the already-absent-tree status.
Use a narrow Windows exclusion for a genuinely POSIX-only primitive, and keep adjacent cross-platform assertions for the product behavior.
Keep supported Windows paths inside the per-file coverage gate rather than excluding the test file.
actors: Test author: chooses native construction.
Fixture owner: provides transport and teardown helpers.
Reviewer: rejects broad platform exclusions.
steps: Replace literal path or URI strings with host API construction.
Assert the output form the contract requires.
For transport failure, inject the writer callback error.
For process trees, use the platform-specific kill and surface real failures.
Exclude only the single impossible fixture; add the neighboring assertion.

enforcement.implementation: Native path and URL construction, writer injection, process-group or taskkill teardown, narrow exclusions with adjacent coverage.
enforcement.trust: The host runtime defines path and URI semantics; the fixture must not normalize them away.
enforcement.failure: A literal POSIX path fails on Windows. A pipe-internal hack tests undocumented machinery. A whole-file exclusion hides supported behavior.
exceptions: A genuinely POSIX-only primitive may exclude that single case on Windows.
Windows teardown may depend on `taskkill` after graceful shutdown fails.

mechanisms.applicability: Cross-platform test suites, especially those with paths, URIs, child pipes and process trees.

migration.strategy: Replace hand-built platform strings and pipe hacks with native APIs and narrow injection points.
migration.implementation: Host path/URL helpers, writer callback injection, platform-specific tree teardown.
migration.requiredSupport: A supported-runtime matrix and a way to run the same suite on each host.

positive: The same semantic test passes on Windows, macOS and Linux.
The transport-failure test keeps a real child alive and distinguishes failure from exit.
rejection: A literal POSIX path under Windows fails or asserts the wrong thing.
A broad Windows exclusion would hide supported behavior.
recovery: If a single POSIX-only state cannot exist, exclude only that case and keep the neighboring assertion.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Native expected paths must derive from shared constants.
Platform-only exclusions need an adjacent cross-platform assertion to remain honest.
Windows tree kill depends on the host command and a failed kill remains visible.

mechanisms.title: Prove the test can fail by reproducing the recorded failure signature with a negative control, then passing the positive control
mechanisms.problem: A test can pass for the wrong reason. Without a control that reproduces the failure, a green run does not show that the assertion observes the property it names, and a threshold or fixture can be calibrated to a state that never exercises the failure.
triggers: A new test claims to guard a specific failure or performance budget.
A fixture was changed to remove a flake.
A threshold or baseline is being chosen.
obligations: Construct a negative control that reproduces the recorded failure signature with the shipped assertions.
Run the positive control after the fix and show it passes.
For performance, measure the baseline and set the budget with explicit headroom; state that the threshold is a regression allowance, not a measurement of what the work needs.
For credentials or matching logic, include both a matching and a non-matching control so the assertion cannot pass on any input.
Record the evidence level: local run, CI run id, or only planned.
Do not infer a failure cause from a single green or red run.
actors: Test author: builds the controls.
Reviewer: checks that the negative control matches the recorded signature, not a convenient failure.
Performance owner: calibrates thresholds.
steps: Write down the observed failure signature.
Reproduce it with the pre-fix fixture or a deliberate wrong input.
Confirm the assertion fails for that reason.
Apply the fix or fixture change.
Confirm the same assertion passes.
Record the runs and rates; repeat under the real topology where the failure was seen.

enforcement.implementation: Before/after controls, deliberately wrong hover or focus, one-clock-only pins, tampered hook config, measured failure rates, threshold headroom.
enforcement.trust: A test is trusted only after it has been shown to fail for the named reason.
enforcement.failure: A test that never fails may be asserting a tautology or a fixture that cannot reach the branch. A threshold set without a measurement can accept a regression or fail on noise.
exceptions: A purely structural assertion may not need a runtime negative control, but it still needs a case that violates the structure.
A proposed mechanism has no executed control and must be marked proposed.

mechanisms.applicability: Every new guard, every flake fix and every performance or security threshold.

migration.strategy: Require a negative control in the change that introduces a guard or fixes a flake.
migration.implementation: A deliberately wrong input, a pre-fix reproduction, a measured before/after table.
migration.requiredSupport: A way to run the pre-fix state or simulate the wrong input without changing production behavior.

positive: The three browser scenarios fail with the recorded signatures under the negative controls and pass after the fix.
The credential-matching test includes a non-matching control.
rejection: A clock test that pins only one clock reproduces the midnight failure exactly.
A threshold without endpoint measurement is rejected.
recovery: Fix the fixture or product and rerun both controls; if the negative control no longer fails, the guard has stopped biting.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes with before/after counts and CI run ids; not re-executed here.

limitations: A negative control can be too artificial and miss the real failure mode.
A local rate is not a CI rate; the topology can differ.
A control proves the assertion can fail, not that it covers every failure.

mechanisms.title: Prefer guards that can bite: fail loud on impossible states and refuse coverage that cannot be proven to fail
mechanisms.problem: A guard that produces byte-identical output to the no-guard run, or that silently skips an extra input, can never be proven to fail. Coverage that includes such guards overstates protection. Silent mis-routing and stale fixtures are worse than an explicit error.
triggers: A test or assertion is proposed for a state that writes nothing or has no observable footprint.
A harness encounters more inputs than recorded scripts or a missing required fixture.
A guard is added for an error path that may never be exercised.
obligations: Make harness states that cannot be routed an explicit fail-loud error, never a silent fallback to another script.
Do not count an observe-only or no-transcript guard as end-to-end coverage; it cannot bite.
Keep a guard on unit coverage when its end-to-end footprint is nondeterministic, and record why it is excluded.
Require every scenario that proves a guard to be shown red when the guarded behavior is removed or tampered.
Distinguish a missing-key skip in a record workflow from a required-gate skip; the required gate must fail loud.
actors: Harness owner: implements fail-loud routing.
Scenario author: proves the guard bites.
Reviewer: rejects guards with no observable footprint.
steps: Check whether the guarded behavior changes the transcript, output or state.
If it does not, keep it at a lower tier and document the omission.
If it does, remove or tamper the behavior and confirm the scenario turns red.
For harness cardinality, compare live and recorded counts and error on excess.
Restore the behavior and confirm green.

enforcement.implementation: Fail-loud on extra live sessions; closed inventories; no-transcript omissions documented; red-to-green checks when a slice or guard is removed.
enforcement.trust: A guard is trusted only if its absence produces a distinguishable failure.
enforcement.failure: A silent fallback mis-routes a child to the parent script. An observe-only expected output equals the no-hook run and can never fail. A guard that only checks presence may pass on the wrong value.
exceptions: An observe-only hook point may remain on unit coverage where the call itself is asserted.
A nondeterministic injection point must not be recorded as a stable golden; a 10/10 replay instability check justifies exclusion.

mechanisms.applicability: Replay harnesses, hook matrices, negative controls and any guard whose expected artifact could be identical with and without the guard.
relationships: Used by replay-script-keying and hook matrix coverage.

migration.strategy: Add fail-loud cardinality checks and document every deliberate exclusion with its reason.
migration.implementation: Count checks, explicit errors, a matrix of covered points, red-to-green evidence per guard.
migration.requiredSupport: A harness that can observe whether a guarded artifact changed.

positive: Tampering a hook config output turns the hook scenario red on replay.
Removing the seed-boundary slice turns both fork scenarios red.
rejection: An observe-only SubagentStop expected output would be byte-identical to the no-hook run and is excluded.
More live sessions than recorded scripts is an error.
recovery: Restore the behavior or the slice and confirm green; if the red state cannot be produced, the guard does not bite.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A guard can bite for the wrong reason; pair it with a signature check.
Some real behavior has no deterministic transcript and cannot be end-to-end guarded.
A fail-loud error can block a legitimate new scenario until it is recorded.

mechanisms.title: Use adversarial property generators for protocol-shaped code, with reproducible seeds and flake treated as a finding
mechanisms.problem: Example tests pin only the cases the author thought of. Protocol code has combinatorial inputs and interleavings. A block-assembly ordering bug once survived 100% line coverage of the happy paths, because coverage proves lines ran, not that interleavings are correct.
triggers: A package has protocol-shaped input: chunk streams, event logs, schema conversion, scheduling.
An example-based suite is approaching a coverage gate but the input space is combinatorial.
A bug appears only for an input interleaving nobody wrote.
obligations: Add one property suite per protocol-shaped package using a property library such as `fast-check`.
Tune generators toward realistic but adversarial inputs (small index pools, short strings, malformed shapes), not uniform noise.
State the invariant for each package: counts, idempotence, determinism, monotonicity, totality, composition with the validator.
Keep `numRuns` bounded so the suite stays fast locally; print a reproducible seed on failure.
Treat a timeout or flake as a finding, not something to retry away; make loop properties deterministic by driving an event or status signal instead of sleeps.
Keep property tests as a supplement to example tests that pin branches for the coverage gate.
actors: Package owner: states invariants and maintains generators.
Test author: adds the property suite.
Reviewer: checks that generators reach the adversarial shapes.
steps: Write a generator for the protocol input.
State the invariant in executable form.
Run a bounded number of cases and print the seed on failure.
On failure, minimize and add a focused regression case.
Keep the suite in the normal test lane; a high-iteration nightly run is separate and optional.

enforcement.implementation: `tests/properties.spec.ts` per package, `fast-check`, bounded `numRuns`, seed output, deterministic settle signals.
enforcement.trust: The invariant, not the example, is the oracle.
enforcement.failure: A generator that produces only valid shapes misses malformed interleavings. A flaky property test indicates a real race or an invalid invariant; retrying hides it.
exceptions: An operation with no meaningful invariant is a poor property target.
A nightly high-iteration job is optional and, in the source, not shipped.
Mutation testing was proposed as a coverage counterweight but is not implemented.

mechanisms.applicability: Protocol-shaped libraries, parsers, assemblers, schedulers and serializers with combinatorial input spaces.
relationships: Supports tripwire-failures by finding a real bug on the first run.
Mutation testing remains a proposed counterweight, not a current mechanism.

migration.strategy: Start with the most algorithmic package, state a small number of invariants, and keep runtime bounded.
migration.implementation: A property library dependency, per-package generators, invariant assertions, seed logging.
migration.requiredSupport: A deterministic driver for asynchronous behavior; a separate optional nightly job if high-iteration runs are wanted.

positive: The BlockAssembler property found a duplicate block-end bug on its first run; the fix added a dedicated regression test.
Session and schema properties assert determinism, monotonicity and totality.
rejection: A 100%-covered happy path did not catch the ordering bug.
A timeout in the loop property is a real hang because the property settles on status, not sleep.
recovery: Minimize the failing seed into an example test and fix the code; keep the property running.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; mutation and nightly stress remain proposed.

limitations: Generator quality is the value lever; weak generators give false confidence.
A property suite does not replace branch-pinning example tests.
Mutation testing and nightly race stress are proposals, not implemented guarantees.

mechanisms.title: Make a required lane fail loudly when its prerequisite is absent; never report green for an unexecuted suite
mechanisms.problem: A suite that self-skips without a secret, or a compatibility lane that runs on only one runtime, can report green while exercising nothing. A one-second check can pass on a fast host and fail on a slow one without measuring the property it names.
triggers: A required workflow depends on a secret, a browser, a runner capability or a runtime version.
A suite self-skips when its prerequisite is missing.
A compatibility claim covers more than one advertised line.
obligations: Separate keyed or capability-dependent work into its own workflow and add a preflight that converts a missing secret or capability into a loud failure.
Do not add a self-skipping suite to an always-green gate; a skip is not evidence.
Run a compatibility smoke on every advertised runtime or platform line, asserting both the conditional configuration and a usable result.
Probe the actual host capability instead of branching only on the platform name; a capability refusal selects the clean fallback case.
State which lane owns the claim and which platforms the gate does not cover.
actors: CI owner: separates workflows and writes the preflight.
Test author: provides capability probes.
Reviewer: checks that a skip cannot satisfy a required verdict.
steps: Identify the prerequisite (secret, browser, system library, runtime flag).
Move the dependent suite to a workflow with the prerequisite.
Add a preflight that fails if the prerequisite is absent.
For compatibility, add a focused smoke per line.
For host capabilities, probe and branch to a clean case.
Record the evidence and the uncovered platforms.

enforcement.implementation: Dedicated keyed workflow, loud missing-secret failure, per-runtime compatibility smoke, capability probe, explicit lane scope.
enforcement.trust: A required gate fails when it cannot execute; a green result means the suite ran.
enforcement.failure: A keyless self-skip reports green without exercising. A single-runtime green leaves other advertised lines unverified. A platform-name branch can run the wrong containment case.
exceptions: A record workflow may self-skip without a key because it is not the required gate.
A capability refusal may select a clean-rejection case and skip the real-dialog case, preserving file coverage.

mechanisms.applicability: PR gates, compatibility matrices, secret-dependent suites and host-capability-dependent tests.
relationships: Uses coverage-plane-honesty to state what a lane does not cover.

migration.strategy: Split always-available and prerequisite-dependent lanes; add preflight before relying on a verdict.
migration.implementation: Workflow separation, preflight step, compatibility smoke, capability probe.
migration.requiredSupport: Secret storage scoped to trusted events and a runtime matrix.

positive: A missing secret in the keyed workflow fails loudly instead of skipping.
Each advertised Node line runs the jsdom smoke and asserts both the worker argument and usable storage.
rejection: A keyless suite added to the always-green gate reports green without running.
A single Node 24 lane would miss a later runtime that reserves `localStorage`.
recovery: Restore the secret or capability and rerun; do not mark the required gate green.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A preflight proves only the prerequisite, not every test outcome.
A capability probe that cannot run keeps the conservative assumption rather than claiming absence.
The gate still cannot cover platforms it does not provision.

mechanisms.title: Keep secrets out of forkable PR execution and restrict the consuming workflow to trusted triggers
mechanisms.problem: A keyless always-green gate cannot consume a repository secret. Fork PRs must not receive the secret. Coupling the secret-consuming job to the always-green gate would either leak the secret or make the gate depend on credential availability.
triggers: A test needs a real API key, signing key or external credential.
A PR can come from a fork.
A workflow is being added to the required gate.
obligations: Put credential-consuming tests in a separate workflow from the always-green PR CI.
Use a repository secret and only trusted event triggers (manual dispatch, pushes to protected branches, schedule, and trusted PR paths).
Do not expose the secret to fork-originated code or to untrusted pull request targets.
Add a preflight that fails when the secret is absent in the keyed workflow.
Do not add the keyless self-skipping suite to the always-green gate as a substitute.
Record the credential lifecycle and who owns rotation.
actors: CI owner: owns workflow triggers and secret scope.
Maintainer: owns the secret.
Reviewer: checks that no untrusted event can reach the credential.
steps: Create a dedicated workflow file with only the credential-consuming tests.
Bind the repository secret.
Restrict triggers to trusted events.
Add the preflight.
Run every matching end-to-end test on each trusted trigger.
Keep the keyless gate separate and always runnable.

enforcement.mode: workflow trigger policy and secret scope
enforcement.implementation: Dedicated `e2e.yml`, repository secret, trusted event filters, preflight, separate keyless `ci.yml`.
enforcement.trust: Only the dedicated workflow may consume the secret; the keyless gate never expects it.
enforcement.failure: Adding the suite to the keyless gate either skips silently or requires the secret on forks. A missing preflight turns a missing secret into a confusing skip.
exceptions: A maintainer-triggered workflow may run on a branch from the same repository.
A record command run locally may use a developer key without CI secret exposure.

mechanisms.applicability: Any repository that runs real external services in CI and accepts fork contributions.
relationships: Supports evidence-scoped-claims about what the keyed lane covers.

migration.strategy: Separate the workflows before adding the credential; restrict triggers first, then add tests.
migration.implementation: A dedicated workflow, trusted event filters, secret binding, preflight.
migration.requiredSupport: Hosting-provider secret scoping and event controls.

positive: The keyed workflow runs on trusted triggers with the repository secret.
The keyless gate stays forkable and always green when tests pass.
rejection: A fork PR cannot read the secret.
A missing secret fails the keyed preflight instead of skipping.
recovery: Restore or rotate the secret and rerun the keyed workflow; do not copy it into the keyless gate.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: A trusted branch can still run untrusted code if the trigger is misconfigured.
A repository secret is not a per-job least-privilege boundary by itself.
The keyed workflow may be skipped on some events by design.

mechanisms.title: Run a dedicated keyed real-API gate on every trusted trigger instead of treating occasional live runs as coverage
mechanisms.problem: Keyless tests can be green while a real ACP session crashes. The policy leaned on real-API tests, but the default `ci.yml` was keyless for forks and the e2e suite self-skips without a key, so adding it to `ci.yml` would report green without exercising anything.
triggers: A product boundary depends on a real external API or service.
A keyless suite has replaced live coverage.
A trusted PR or nightly run should exercise the real service.
obligations: Create a dedicated keyed workflow that runs every matching end-to-end test.
Run it on manual dispatch, pushes to protected branches, a nightly schedule, and every trusted PR.
Treat cost as secondary to reliability for this lane; do not narrow it to keep it cheap.
Keep the keyless gate separate and always available.
State that the keyed lane is not the same as a full matrix of every platform and service.
actors: CI owner: owns triggers and scope.
Maintainer: owns the key.
Reviewer: checks that trusted PRs actually run the lane.
steps: Create `e2e.yml` with only the end-to-end command.
Bind the repository secret and restrict triggers.
Run on the agreed events.
Keep the preflight loud.
Record failures as real defects, not as flaky retries.

enforcement.implementation: `e2e.yml`, `test:e2e`, repository secret, trusted event filters, nightly schedule.
enforcement.trust: The real service is the oracle; the keyless suite is not a substitute.
enforcement.failure: A keyless skip can look green. A fork cannot run the keyed lane by design. A missing key must fail the preflight.
exceptions: A contributor without a key can still run keyless tests locally.
A record workflow may self-skip without a key; the required keyed gate may not.

mechanisms.applicability: Projects with a real external service that cannot be exercised on untrusted PRs but must be covered continuously.
relationships: Complements record-once-replay-corpus: replay for deterministic breadth, live for the real boundary.

migration.strategy: Stand up the keyed workflow and preflight before relying on live coverage claims.
migration.implementation: Dedicated workflow, triggers, secret, preflight, full e2e command.
migration.requiredSupport: A secret store, trusted-event configuration and a stable live test suite.

positive: Every matching end-to-end file runs on every trusted trigger.
The live lane catches a real boundary failure that keyless tests cannot.
rejection: Adding the self-skipping suite to `ci.yml` would report green without exercising.
A missing secret in the keyed lane is a loud failure.
recovery: Fix the product or the live fixture and rerun; do not downgrade the lane to a skip.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Live runs are nondeterministic and can fail for external reasons.
The lane covers only the services and platforms it provisions.
Cost and credential ownership remain operational concerns.

mechanisms.title: Treat probabilistic failure as a defect to diagnose, with an owned isolation and flake workflow
mechanisms.problem: Tests run across concurrent files, workers, gates and jobs. Process isolation does not isolate host resources. Global mutations and incomplete teardown contaminate later tests. A test can pass only when run alone. Existing policy, defensive patterns and review give no focused workflow for designing resource-owning tests or classifying a probabilistic failure before changing code.
triggers: A test acquires host resources, mutates process-global state, depends on asynchronous readiness, owns subprocesses or listeners, or fails only sometimes.
A flake is proposed to be fixed by retry, a larger timeout or a skip.
A CI failure cannot be reproduced locally.
obligations: Model the concurrency the test meets and the resources it owns before choosing a fix.
Classify the failure: deterministic product bug, test isolation defect, timing/readiness defect, host capacity, or external service.
Fix the ownership or observation, not the symptom; do not retry, widen a budget or skip to make a flake disappear.
Record the evidence and reproduction rate; a single run does not establish a cause.
Keep a focused authoring and diagnosis guide as the current reference, and distinguish it from proposed mechanisms it does not implement.
Require teardown and budget ownership to be explicit in review.
actors: Test author: models resources and reproduces the failure.
CI owner: provides topology and logs.
Reviewer: rejects masking fixes.
steps: Reproduce under the real topology or record the failure rate.
Identify the shared resource or missing observation.
Apply the ownership or barrier fix.
Add a negative control or repeat run showing the failure is gone for the named reason.
Update the guide if the failure class is new.

enforcement.mode: review policy and a maintained guide
enforcement.implementation: A CI test reliability guide or Skill, resource inventory, flake classification, prohibition of retry-based masking, explicit budget ownership.
enforcement.trust: The guide is current guidance; proposed mechanisms it does not implement are not obligations.
enforcement.failure: A retry hides the cause. A widened budget hides a capacity problem. A skip hides a supported path. A fix without reproduction may change the wrong thing.
exceptions: An external-service outage may be retried only under an explicitly stated policy, not as a general test fix.
A proposed governance mechanism remains proposed until implemented.

mechanisms.applicability: Any multi-worker test system, especially one with subprocesses, network listeners and shared CI hosts.

migration.strategy: Adopt the resource model and failure classification before changing individual tests.
migration.implementation: A maintained guide, resource inventory, reproduction-rate evidence, review checklist.
migration.requiredSupport: CI logs that preserve failure context and a way to run the real concurrent topology.

positive: A resource-owning test is designed with its concurrency and cleanup stated.
A probabilistic failure is classified and fixed with evidence.
rejection: A retry-only fix and a larger timeout are rejected as masking.
A test that passes alone but fails in the lane is treated as an isolation defect, not a flake to retry.
recovery: Reproduce, fix ownership or observation, then rerun under the real topology; record the rate.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; the guide itself was referenced but not inspected in this partition.

limitations: A guide is not an automatic checker.
Some failures depend on host capacity outside the test control.
A proposed lint rule, universal replay fixture or nightly stress job is not implemented and must not be claimed.

mechanisms.title: Gate measured user paths with endpoint budgets, isolated seeds and fresh workers, and keep the budget under real memory pressure
mechanisms.problem: A performance regression can reach master unnoticed: first open regressed from 35ms to 5s on a 127,400-event synthetic log and from 0.3s to 26s on a 575,000-chunk real log, with 2.7GB RSS and heap exhaustion at a 512MB limit. A single `open()` measurement is insufficient because work moves among open, read, restore and projection, and endpoint heap usage without GC cannot separate retained from reclaimable memory. Uniform small corpora also understate heavy-tailed real sessions.
triggers: A user-visible path has a latency or memory contract.
A change can move work between lifecycle stages rather than remove it.
A benchmark or threshold is being added or changed.
obligations: Measure a compiled production path under plain Node, with no TypeScript loader and with ambient `NODE_OPTIONS` removed.
Group gates by the measured user path, not by internal module; measure endpoints of a workflow rather than independent cold scenarios when the user experiences them together.

Author current-generation sessions through the production append/stream/persistence path in a separate seed process; each sample copies to a private root and runs a fresh worker; fix timestamps and ids in the seed.
Set endpoint budgets with explicit headroom, for example a 50ms standard-runner expectation with 1.25x headroom giving 63ms.
Retain raw samples in verbose gate output; threshold changes require measured calibration and both positive and negative controls.
Run the same benchmark files under a cgroup memory clamp (for example 4 or 8 GiB with swap zero) and require the normal budget or treat a cgroup kill as failure.
Keep benchmark-only dependencies in a private workspace so the product install is unchanged.
actors: Performance owner: owns workloads, budgets and calibration.
Benchmark author: authors the seed and scenario.
CI: provisions the runner and retains raw samples.
Reviewer: rejects unmeasured threshold changes.
steps: Author the workload from production code and real distribution anchors.
Build the artifacts, then benchmark compiled output.
Seed a private copy per sample and start a fresh worker.
Measure every endpoint of the workflow.
Calibrate a budget with headroom and record the raw measurement.
Re-run under memory pressure and confirm the budget still holds.

enforcement.implementation: `check:ci:bench` / `run-ci-bench.ts`, `vitest.bench.config.ts`, `benchmarks/**/*.bench.ts` and `*.bench.client.ts`, compiled JS under plain Node, private workspace deps, cgroup v2 `memory.max` with zero swap.
enforcement.trust: The budget is a regression allowance derived from endpoint measurement, not a theoretical target.
enforcement.failure: A budget without endpoint measurement is rejected. A cgroup kill or a normal-budget miss fails the case. A single cold scenario can hide work moved to another stage.
exceptions: Package-local `.perf.ts` files are non-gating diagnostics.
A hardware-comparison workflow may use deliberately different runner sizes but does not replace the standard gate.
Terminal, fold, reconnect and continuation workloads may be excluded from the memory clamp when they are small in-process.

mechanisms.applicability: Projects with a user-visible latency or memory contract and enough benchmark infrastructure to run compiled production paths.
relationships: Uses perf-diagnostics-separation to keep stress evidence out of the gate.
Requires evidence-scoped-claims for what the measurement covers.

migration.strategy: Start from one measured user path, then expand by endpoint and workload; keep a clean standard runner class.
migration.implementation: A benchmark build, seed process, fresh-worker harness, endpoint budgets, verbose raw samples, memory-clamp runner.
migration.requiredSupport: A standard hosted runner class, benchmark-only dependencies and a corpus with recorded provenance.

positive: The session-open gate catches the 35ms-to-5s and 0.3s-to-26s regressions.
The corpus benchmark anchors 1,650 real sessions by upper quantiles and measures list, search and fork endpoints.
rejection: A threshold raised without endpoint measurement is rejected.
A cgroup kill or a normal-budget miss under the memory clamp fails the case.
recovery: Fix the regression or recalibrate with measured evidence; do not relax the budget silently.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: A benchmark budget measures a runner class, not every machine.
A synthetic corpus is not production content.
Memory-clamp behavior at 4 or 8 GiB does not generalize to all deployments.

mechanisms.title: Keep stress lanes and manual benchmarks as scoped evidence, separate from deterministic gates
mechanisms.problem: A browser stress lane measured through a real transport can be overwhelmed by socket backlog, and hardware or scheduling variation makes it unsuitable as a pass/fail gate. Conversely, a deterministic unit test cannot show responsiveness. Mixing the two either blocks merges on noise or hides a real performance defect.
triggers: A performance claim needs a real assembled application and transport.
A stress or benchmark lane is proposed as a required check.
A result is being used to claim responsiveness or capacity.
obligations: Label stress and profiling lanes as explicit evidence for manual diagnosis and fix acceptance, not default CI gates.
Pace the producer with an acknowledgment so the measurement is one bounded ingestion/render interval, not accumulated transport backlog.
Include a terminal marker proving all input reached the UI, and preserve exact event counts.
Use a test-owned adapter through the real Host and transport rather than an external nondeterministic model or a second HTTP recording format.
Keep deterministic focused tests for publication counts, accumulated content, preemption order and fallbacks.
Retain raw samples and verbose output in the required benchmark job; separate hardware-comparison workflows.
actors: Performance author: designs the stress or benchmark scenario.
CI owner: decides gate versus evidence.
Reviewer: rejects gate use without a bounded topology.
steps: Decide whether the claim is deterministic correctness or responsiveness evidence.
For stress, pace batches with a browser-timer acknowledgment and a heartbeat.
Emit a terminal marker and count every event.
Run manually or as opt-in evidence; profile with the headful mode.
Keep deterministic assertions in the normal suite.

enforcement.implementation: Opt-in `test:web:stress`, 128-chunk batches with a timer acknowledgment, 50ms heartbeat, 250ms budget, terminal marker, `DSH_WEB_STRESS_HEADFUL=1`, focused Notifier/Session tests.
enforcement.trust: Stress results are evidence, not a merge verdict. Deterministic focused tests own the publication contract.
enforcement.failure: Pacing by animation frames gives the page implicit backpressure and masks starvation. Sending without acknowledgment measures socket backlog. An external model adds nondeterminism. A stress lane as a gate blocks on hardware noise.
exceptions: A benchmark with a measured endpoint and fixed runner class may be a required gate; that is performance-budget-gate, not this evidence lane.
A visible profiling run may use the same scenario with different observation.

mechanisms.applicability: Responsiveness, throughput or long-stream stress where the real assembled stack matters but the result varies by hardware and scheduling.

migration.strategy: Keep the stress lane opt-in and explicitly labeled; add deterministic tests for the mechanism before claiming coverage.
migration.implementation: A paced producer, timer acknowledgment, terminal marker, headful profiling switch, focused publication tests.
migration.requiredSupport: A real Host and transport in the test environment and a way to opt into the lane.

positive: 100,000 reasoning chunks reach the UI and the terminal marker proves delivery.
Focused tests pin per-frame coalescing, preemption, invalidated callbacks and no-rAF fallback.
rejection: Animation-frame pacing would slow the producer and hide main-thread starvation.
Without acknowledgment the measurement becomes socket backlog.
recovery: Use the headful profiler to diagnose; keep the deterministic tests green.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Hardware and scheduling differences make the lane unsuitable as a default gate.
It reduces snapshot rebuilding and React work, not raw-stream parsing cost.
A terminal marker proves delivery, not responsiveness for every user.

mechanisms.title: Scope every test and benchmark claim to the topology actually exercised, and mark the rest planned
mechanisms.problem: A green run on one runtime, platform, runner class or corpus is often reported as if it covered all of them. A local measurement is not a CI measurement; a single developer corpus is not production; a capability probe that cannot run is not proof of absence; a note describing a mechanism is not proof that it executes.
triggers: A change description, comment or review claims coverage, performance or cross-platform consistency.
A test skips, probes or samples a subset.
A benchmark runs on one runner or one corpus.
obligations: State the exact runtime, platform, runner class, corpus and topology a result covers.
Do not generalize a local result to CI, a single-machine corpus to production, or one browser to cross-platform consistency.
Keep raw samples and run identifiers so the claim can be audited.
Mark unexercised claims as planned or unknown rather than passed.
A capability probe that cannot run keeps the conservative assumption; a probe refusal selects only the corresponding fallback case.
Distinguish source-report evidence from independently re-executed evidence.
actors: Test author: writes the scoped claim.
Reviewer: rejects overgeneralization.
CI owner: preserves run ids and logs.
steps: Name the topology and the exact assertion.
Record run ids, counts and raw samples.
List what the run does not cover.
If a claim depends on another domain or an uninspected target, mark it unbound.
Re-run only when the claim is exercised; otherwise keep it planned.

enforcement.implementation: Scoped issue/PR text, run ids, raw benchmark samples, explicit non-coverage notes, `evidenceStatus` in this knowledge base.
enforcement.trust: Only the exercised topology supports the claim.
enforcement.failure: A local green reported as CI coverage is false. A fixed-runner benchmark reported as universal is false. A YAML assertion reported as host capacity is false.
exceptions: A deliberately broad platform claim may be supported by a matrix, but then each line must be listed.
A historical note may report its own run; that is source-report evidence, not this extraction running it.

mechanisms.applicability: Every test, benchmark, audit and migration claim.
relationships: Used by every mechanism verification block.

migration.strategy: Add a scope-and-limitations section to every claim; keep unknown and planned states visible.
migration.implementation: Run-id recording, raw samples, per-platform matrices, explicit evidence status.
migration.requiredSupport: Log retention and a review norm that rejects unqualified claims.

positive: The web gate states it makes no cross-platform browser consistency claim.
The benchmark note states that a runner change needs an actual hosted run before the timeout is validated.
rejection: Local workflow assertions alone cannot establish execution time.
A single developer corpus cannot be presented as production content.
recovery: Run the missing topology or downgrade the claim to planned; do not fill the gap with inference.
verification.evidenceStatus: this mechanism is a reporting obligation; all mechanism evidence here is source-reported and not re-executed.

limitations: Scoping does not create evidence.
A correctly scoped weak test is still weak.
Historical run ids can expire or become unreadable.

mechanisms.title: Measure coverage only on the plane the gate can honestly see, and put gate-worthy logic there
mechanisms.problem: A per-file 100% coverage gate scoped to package sources does not measure browser-driving code, test harnesses or support modules. Mechanisms can sit entirely outside the measured plane while appearing covered, and a package test can be mistaken for product coverage after the product entry point is removed.
triggers: A coverage gate is defined by a path glob.
Test or harness code carries logic that could regress.
A package test is proposed as evidence for an assembled application.
obligations: State the exact path plane the coverage gate measures and the logic it does not measure.
Move gate-worthy logic into measured packages; keep browser-driving or harness code outside only when per-file coverage would be dishonest.
Do not claim product coverage from package tests after the product composition is removed; name the deployment that owns the assembled layer.
Keep narrow platform exclusions inside the file coverage gate rather than excluding the file.
Add a compatibility smoke per advertised runtime line so one lane is not the only signal.
Report uncovered planes as limitations, not as hidden gaps.
actors: Coverage owner: defines the path plane.
Test author: places logic where the gate can see it.
Reviewer: rejects product-coverage claims from package tests.
steps: List the measured paths and the excluded harness paths.
Move pure, decision-bearing logic into a measured package.
Keep only the driver or environment glue outside.
Document the excluded plane and who owns it.
Add per-line or per-platform smokes where a single lane would otherwise be the only signal.

enforcement.implementation: Per-file 100% coverage over `packages/*/*/src`, harness code outside the gate, explicit scope notes, compatibility smokes, narrow per-case exclusions.
enforcement.trust: Coverage is evidence only for the measured plane.
enforcement.failure: A mechanism in an unmeasured harness appears covered by its consumers. A package snapshot after entry-point removal is not product coverage. A single-runtime green leaves other advertised lines unmeasured.
exceptions: Browser-driving code cannot honestly hold per-file 100%; keep the gate-worthy logic in gated packages.
A package-local snapshot still guards its package contract even though it does not guard the assembled deployment.

mechanisms.applicability: Monorepos and layered products where test harnesses, examples and drivers sit outside the coverage glob.
relationships: Explains why replay-assembled-lane and semantic-state-projection have separate ownership boundaries.

migration.strategy: Define the measured plane and move decision logic into it before claiming coverage.
migration.implementation: Coverage path configuration, package placement rules, explicit scope documentation, per-runtime smokes.
migration.requiredSupport: A coverage tool that reports per file and a package layout that can host the logic.

positive: Gate-worthy logic lives in measured packages and is covered per file.
Each advertised runtime line runs a focused compatibility smoke.
rejection: A support package outside the glob cannot be counted as product coverage.
A package TUI snapshot cannot substitute for an assembled application tool-path transcript.
recovery: Move the logic or document the uncovered plane; do not report the gate as covering it.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: Coverage still proves lines execute, not that assertions notice errors.
Moving logic can increase coupling; the placement is a design decision.
A per-file gate can encourage shallow tests if used as the only quality signal.

mechanisms.title: Inject distinct faults at the real boundary and assert the recovery policy separately from the fault description
mechanisms.problem: Connection refusal, reset before the first event, clean EOF without a terminator, a valid content-less completion and a reset after partial output have different adapter and recovery outcomes. Treating them as one generic failure hides whether the boundary preserved the distinction and whether failed chunks stayed outside committed history.
triggers: An adapter, updater, network client or process supervisor has a recovery policy.
A test needs to prove that a transient fault recovers and a deterministic fault does not.
A fault taxonomy exists but tests collapse it.
obligations: Implement a scriptable fault source at the real boundary with one explicit behavior per accepted request.
Make script exhaustion loud; require an explicit repeat marker for repetition.
Preserve each fault class distinctly and assert its adapter classification separately from its recovery.
Run the shipping adapter, loop and retry policy through the fault source; assert request counts, step numbers, body identity and failed-chunk isolation.
For a random stress profile, expose and log the seed and accept caller-supplied weights; state that weights are test pressure, not incident frequency.
A true connection refusal may need a listener-lifecycle phase because a bound handler cannot refuse its own connection.
Do not change the retry policy in the fault harness; policy changes require a separate decision.
actors: Test-infrastructure owner: maintains the fault source.
Adapter owner: owns classification.
Retry owner: owns recovery policy.
steps: Enumerate the fault classes and their expected classification.
Implement each as an explicit script entry.
Drive the shipping stack with an explicit script.
Assert classification, request count, retry steps and isolation of failed output.
Add a seeded random profile for stress, logging the seed.
Keep recovery assertions separate from class assertions.

enforcement.mode: shared fault harness and integration suite
enforcement.implementation: `dsh-llm-mock-server` with request behaviors, CLI listener phase for refusal, `repeatLast`, seeded weighted random profile; updater loopback feed; cgroup memory clamp.
enforcement.trust: The fault source reports wire facts; the shipping stack decides retryability.
enforcement.failure: A generic mock hides a distinction. A random profile without a seed is not reproducible. A harness that changes policy conflates observation with a product decision.
exceptions: An in-process adapter mock may still test closed-step recovery, but it cannot cover wire framing.
A platform-specific updater or installer may need a private fixture that omits publisher verification; that omission must be stated.

mechanisms.applicability: Adapters, updaters, network clients and supervisors with a documented fault taxonomy and recovery policy.

migration.strategy: Build the explicit fault vocabulary first, then wire the shipping stack through it.
migration.implementation: A private fault server with per-request behaviors, a seed and weights, and integration assertions for counts and isolation.
migration.requiredSupport: A local peer the shipping adapter can reach and a way to script responses.

positive: Refusal, hard disconnect, partial reset, idle timeout and valid content-less completion recover under the existing policy.
Clean partial EOF stays `STREAM_CLOSED` and is not retried by default.
rejection: A single generic failure would hide which classes recover.
A fault harness that changed retry defaults would make the observation self-fulfilling.
recovery: Add the missing class or script entry; keep policy changes in a separate decision.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source notes; not re-executed here.

limitations: The harness reports wire facts, not production incident frequency.
A random profile needs a seed and is still not a production distribution.
Exact refusal requires coordinating the client attempt with the pre-listen interval.
Installer qualification may be platform-specific.

mechanisms.title: Retry only a named transient failure, with a small bounded budget, and let deterministic failures fail immediately
mechanisms.problem: A CI install step can fail on an intermittent network timeout unrelated to the change, with no recovery beyond a human rerun. Unbounded or broad retries hide real failures and waste time; no retry at all turns an external transient into a red gate.
triggers: A workflow step depends on an external download, registry or service.
A failure is observed to be transient and carries a recognizable error.
A retry is proposed for a test or build step.
obligations: Name the transient failure class and the step it affects.
Set a small total attempt budget and a fixed pause; succeed on any attempt and stop immediately.
Keep a deterministic failure (license, lockfile, configuration, compile error) failing even after the full budget.
Use a portable shell on every platform image.
Do not apply this to test assertions or performance gates; a test flake is a finding, not a retry target.
Record the residual failure path so a human can still diagnose an exhausted budget.
actors: CI owner: implements and bounds the retry.
Reviewer: checks it cannot mask a deterministic failure.
Operator: diagnoses an exhausted budget.
steps: Identify the transient error signature and the step.
Wrap the command in a bounded loop with a pause.
Exit immediately on success.
Keep deterministic errors outside the transient classification or let them exhaust the budget and fail.
Record the final failure with the attempts.

enforcement.implementation: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` retried up to three total attempts with a 10s pause, bash on every platform, immediate success exit.
enforcement.trust: Only the named transient class is retried; the command itself is unchanged.
enforcement.failure: A broad retry hides a lockfile or native-build failure. An unbounded retry wastes capacity and obscures the cause. Retrying a test flake hides a product or test defect.
exceptions: An external-service outage may justify a bounded retry under an explicit policy.
A test flake is never fixed by retry; use negative-control-calibration and test-reliability-governance.

mechanisms.applicability: CI installs, downloads and other steps with a known intermittent external dependency.
relationships: Contrasts with timeout-budgeting, which raises a budget rather than repeating work.

migration.strategy: Add a bounded retry only after observing and naming the transient failure.
migration.implementation: A shell loop with three attempts and a 10s pause, immediate success exit.
migration.requiredSupport: A portable shell on all runners and a logged final error.

positive: A transient node-gyp connect timeout is retried and the install can succeed.
A deterministic native-build error still fails after the bounded budget.
rejection: An unbounded retry or a retry around the test command is rejected.
A lockfile error masked by retry would be a false pass.
recovery: After the final attempt, fail with the captured error; a human diagnoses the external service.
verification.evidenceStatus: reported in source note; not re-executed here.

limitations: Retries add wall time and can mask a persistent external degradation.
The classification depends on the observed error text.
This does not make the external service reliable.
